knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Active Constraint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak activity is defined relative to a specified KKT multiplier when multipliers are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a KKT pair \((x^*,\lambda^*)\), define \(I_0(x^*,\lambda^*)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:G_ix^*=h_i,\ \lambda_i^*=0\}\) and \(I_+(x^*,\lambda^*)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:G_ix^*=h_i,\ \lambda_i^*>0\}\). Members of \(I_0(x^*,\lambda^*)\) are weakly active. If KKT multipliers are nonunique, the partition into weakly and strongly active constraints may depend on the selected multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a selected KKT certificate, a weakly active inequality binds but has zero multiplier; under multiplier nonuniqueness, this classification can depend on the certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\), \(h\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and \((x^*,\lambda^*)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\) satisfies the KKT conditions for constraints \(Gx\leq h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A constraint \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) is weakly active relative to \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) exactly when \(G_ix^*=h_i\) and \(\lambda_i^*=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasible active-set ascent for a strictly convex primal quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with \(\lambda_0\geq0\) and a working set \(W_0\) containing its positive components. Maximize \(D\) over coordinates in \(W_k\), keeping \(\lambda_{\bar W_k}=0\). If the step toward the restricted maximizer would make a working multiplier negative, truncate at the first zero component and remove that index. Otherwise accept the restricted maximizer. If some inactive coordinate has \(\nabla_iD(\lambda_k)=G_ix(\lambda_k)-h_i>0\), add such an index; stop when every inactive dual gradient is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method maintains nonnegative multipliers, optimizes the concave dual over a working set, and adds coordinates with violated dual optimality.

Reclassify the constraints using the same rule. Stop when the partition is unchanged and the computed pair satisfies primal feasibility and dual nonnegativity; otherwise repeat. The output is the final primal-dual pair and its active-set estimate.

children.title: Primal Iterate Warm Starts
children.top_down_role: Reuse of prior primal solutions or trial points when initializing related QP subproblems.

assumptions_latex: A previous primal iterate \(\bar x\) and new feasible polyhedron \(C=\{x:Gx\leq h\}\neq\varnothing\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The initialized point \(x_0\) is feasible and is the unique \(R\)-metric projection of \(\bar x\) onto the new feasible set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal initialization and working-set seeding for a changed inequality QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G\bar x\leq h\), set \(x_0=\bar x\); otherwise compute \(x_0=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12(x-\bar x)^\top R(x-\bar x)\). Seed the working set by \(W_0=\{i:h_i-G_ix_0\leq\tau\}\), optionally retaining only a linearly independent subset when the equality subproblem solver requires one. Pass \((x_0,W_0)\) to the primal working-set method. The warm start is accepted only after explicitly checking \(Gx_0\leq h\); otherwise feasibility restoration must continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the previous primal iterate onto the new feasible polyhedron, then seed the working set with constraints whose new slacks are small.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization interface for consecutive inequality-constrained quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a quadratic program with equalities and inequalities, and let \(W_0\) be the initial working set inherited from a preceding solve. Given preceding multipliers \((\lambda^{\mathrm{old}},\mu^{\mathrm{old}})\), initialize equality multipliers by \(\lambda^0=\lambda^{\mathrm{old}}\). For each inequality \(i\in W_0\), set \(\mu_i^0=\max\{0,\mu_i^{\mathrm{old}}\}\), and set \(\mu_i^0=0\) for \(i\notin W_0\). If constraints were added, removed, or reordered, first map multipliers by persistent constraint identifiers. The active-set solver then tests primal feasibility, dual signs, and stationarity; the warm start supplies initialization only and is not itself a KKT certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map persistent old multipliers to the new working set, project inequality multipliers onto nonnegative values, and let the solver restore full KKT consistency.
assumptions_latex: \(W_0\) contains only inequalities present in the new quadratic program.
Inequalities use the convention \(c_i(x)\ge 0\), so their KKT multipliers are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\lambda^0,\mu^0)\) is a well-defined multiplier initialization, but need not be primal-dual feasible or stationary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard active-set QP warm-start convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the warm-start interface, and the statement correctly avoids treating the initialization as a KKT certificate. However, multiplier transfer, sign projection, and handling of changed equality constraints are solver- and convention-dependent; no inspectable authoritative source is supplied to establish this exact policy.

children.title: Working-Set Reuse
children.top_down_role: Transfer of active-set structure across nearby or sequential QP subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Working-Set Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse rule for a sequence of closely related active-set quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W^{\mathrm{old}}\) be the final working set from a preceding quadratic program and let \(I_{\mathrm{new}}\) index the inequalities in the new problem. Form \(W_0=W^{\mathrm{old}}\cap I_{\mathrm{new}}\) after mapping persistent constraint identifiers. Remove any member incompatible with the supplied initial primal point, and optionally add every inequality violated by that point. Initialize the equality-constrained subproblem on \(W_0\). Thereafter apply the ordinary active-set rules: add a blocking constraint when a step is truncated, and delete a working inequality whose multiplier violates the required sign. Terminate only when primal feasibility and the KKT sign conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filter the preceding active set to valid current constraints, repair it for the new primal point, then resume ordinary add-and-delete active-set iterations.
assumptions_latex: Successive problems provide persistent identifiers for unchanged constraints.
The active-set solver supports an arbitrary admissible initial working set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction yields a valid initialization interface without asserting that the reused set is optimal for the new problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and local scope are appropriate, but the proposed removal and optional addition rules are implementation-specific. In particular, adding constraints violated by the supplied point does not by itself produce a feasible primal active-set initialization. An authoritative locator is needed for the intended solver interface and repair procedure.

children.title: Warm-Start Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problem changes that make inherited iterates, multipliers, or working sets unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A maximal active-face change showing that warm starts need not be informative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), consider minimizing \(q_s(x)=\tfrac12\lVert x-s\rVert_2^2\) over \([0,1]^n\). With \(s=-\mathbf 1\), the unique solution is \(x^-=0\), and every lower bound is active with a positive multiplier. After changing the parameter to \(s=2\mathbf 1\), the unique solution is \(x^+=\mathbf 1\), and every upper bound is active instead. Thus the preceding primal solution, working set, and nonzero bound multipliers can all be incorrect for the new problem. Warm-start reuse therefore has no unconditional proximity, active-set accuracy, or iteration-saving guarantee when problem data change without a quantitative perturbation restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter change can switch every active lower bound to an active upper bound, making the old primal point, working set, and multipliers maximally misleading.
assumptions_latex: Warm-start information is transferred without a bound on the change in \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No data-independent guarantee of active-set agreement or reduced iteration count follows from warm starting alone.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is exact, and the separable quadratic example supports the claimed absence of unconditional active-set agreement. The signs of the asserted bound multipliers depend on an unstated constraint and Lagrangian convention, and no source is supplied for the broader warm-start guarantee boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(A_W\) contains the current equality and working-inequality rows.
The current KKT matrix \(K_W\) is nonsingular before the proposed update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted updates factor the new KKT matrix; a failed pivot or stability test triggers full refactorization rather than an unsafe update.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bordered KKT factorization update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bordered updates for equality-constrained systems arising after one working-set change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a working set \(W\), form the symmetric KKT matrix \(K_W=\begin{pmatrix}H&A_W^{\mathsf T}\\A_W&0\end{pmatrix}\) and maintain a permutation-aware \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) factorization. When one independent constraint row \(a^{\mathsf T}\) enters, represent \(K_{W\cup\{a\}}\) as a one-row-and-column bordered matrix and extend the factors using triangular solves and the resulting Schur-complement pivot. When one constraint leaves, symmetrically permute its row and column to a removable position and downdate or refactor the affected trailing block. Reject an update and refactorize whenever the pivot test indicates rank loss or unacceptable numerical stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain the working-set KKT factorization by bordered additions and symmetric deletions, but refactorize when rank or stability tests fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Working-Set Factorization Updates

children.title: Gradient Projection for Bound-Constrained QP Subproblems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Stage Gradient Projection for Box-Constrained Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithmic structure for a symmetric, possibly indefinite box-constrained quadratic program, together with a conditional active-set iteration boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{q(x)=\tfrac12x^T Gx+c^Tx:l\le x\le u\}\), where \(G=G^T\) need not be positive definite and absent lower or upper bounds may be represented by \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\). From a feasible current point \(x\), with \(g=Gx+c\), the first stage follows the feasible piecewise-linear path formed by bending \(-g\) at encountered bounds and searches for its first local minimizer \(x^c\). The working set is then \(\mathcal A(x^c)\), and the second stage approximately minimizes \(q\) on the box face obtained by fixing \(x_i=x_i^c\) for \(i\in\mathcal A(x^c)\). Separately, if an active-set scheme starts with no active constraints, can add at most one active constraint per iteration, and reaches a nondegenerate solution having \(m\) active constraints, then it requires at least \(m\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient-projection iteration for a symmetric, possibly indefinite box-constrained quadratic program first searches the projected steepest-descent path for its first local minimizer, then approximately minimizes on the box face determined by the bounds active there. Conditionally, an active-set scheme that can add at most one active constraint per iteration needs at least m iterations to reach a nondegenerate solution with m active constraints when none are initially active.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the iteration bound: }\mathcal A(x^0)=\varnothing,\ \lvert\mathcal A(x^*)\rvert=m,\ x^*\text{ is nondegenerate, and at most one active constraint is added per iteration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration searches first along the projected-gradient path and then over the face determined by }\mathcal A(x^c);\qquad N_{\mathrm{AS}}\ge m\text{ under the stated active-set assumptions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face-Subproblem Acceptance Condition in Gradient Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded second-stage face minimization and the inexact acceptance condition used by the bound-constrained QP gradient-projection procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After computing \(x^c\), define \(\mathcal A(x^c)=\{i:x_i^c=l_i\text{ or }x_i^c=u_i\}\). The second stage approximately solves \[\min_x q(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx+c^Tx\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_i=x_i^c\ \ (i\in\mathcal A(x^c)),\qquad l_i\le x_i\le u_i\ \ (i\notin\mathcal A(x^c)).\] Within the stated gradient-projection procedure, exact face minimization is not required for its global-convergence argument: the returned point \(x^+\) need only satisfy \(l\le x^+\le u\) and \(q(x^+)\le q(x^c)\). Conjugate gradient on the reduced equality-constrained problem is one proposed way to seek such a point; it may be stopped when a new bound is encountered, or an unconstrained reduced iterate may be projected back onto the box. Negative curvature requires the corresponding indefinite-subproblem handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second stage fixes the variables active at the Cauchy point and approximately minimizes over the resulting box face. For the convergence argument described in the extract, exact face minimization is unnecessary: the accepted point must remain box-feasible and must not increase the objective relative to the Cauchy point. Reduced conjugate gradient is a proposed implementation, with separate handling for newly encountered bounds and negative curvature.
assumptions_latex: \text{The condition is applied as the second-stage requirement within the stated gradient-projection procedure}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: l\le x^+\le u\quad\text{and}\quad q(x^+)\le q(x^c)\quad\text{are the required inexact second-stage acceptance conditions in the stated convergence argument.}

children.title: Box Projection Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure of projection onto lower and upper variable bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Box Projection Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto a finite box, including its normal-cone characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=[l,u]=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:l_i\le x_i\le u_i\}\), where \(l_i<u_i\). For every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), the Euclidean projection is unique and satisfies \([P_B(z)]_i=\min\{u_i,\max\{l_i,z_i\}\}\). Equivalently, \(y=P_B(z)\) if and only if \(y\in B\) and \(\langle z-y,v-y\rangle\le 0\) for every \(v\in B\), or \(z-y\in N_B(y)\). Moreover, projection is firmly nonexpansive: \(\lVert P_B(z)-P_B(w)\rVert_2^2\le\langle P_B(z)-P_B(w),z-w\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a box clips each coordinate; equivalently, its residual lies in the box normal cone, and the projection is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clipping formula, variational inequality, and normal-cone inclusion characterize the same unique point \(P_B(z)\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to the box at y

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise Box Projection and Projected Gradient Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of projection onto coordinate bounds and its use in the projected-gradient path for a box-constrained quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(l_i<u_i\), allowing an absent lower or upper bound to be represented by \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\). Define \[P(y,l,u)_i=\begin{cases}l_i,&y_i<l_i,\\y_i,&y_i\in[l_i,u_i],\\u_i,&y_i>u_i.\end{cases}\] For \(q(z)=\tfrac12z^TGz+c^Tz\) with \(G=G^T\), a reference point \(x\), and \(g=Gx+c\), the projected steepest-descent path is \(x(t)=P(x-tg,l,u)\) for \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a box clamps each coordinate to its lower or upper bound when necessary and otherwise leaves it unchanged. Applying this projection to the ray x minus t times the quadratic gradient gives a feasible piecewise-linear path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(y,l,u)_i=\min\{u_i,\max\{l_i,y_i\}\},\qquad x(t)=P(x-tg,l,u)\text{ is feasible and piecewise linear.}

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Gradient Mapping Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity residual for differentiable minimization over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable function \(q:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\), a box \(B=[l,u]\), and \(\alpha>0\), define \(G_\alpha(x)=\alpha^{-1} igl(x-P_B(x-\alpha
abla q(x)) igr)\) for \(x\in B\). The projection variational inequality gives \(G_\alpha(x)=0\) if and only if \(-
abla q(x)\in N_B(x)\), equivalently \(0\in
abla q(x)+N_B(x)\). Hence zeros of \(G_\alpha\) are exactly first-order stationary points on the box, independently of the chosen positive \(\alpha\). Its norm is therefore a computable stationarity residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected-gradient mapping measures displacement after a projected gradient step, and it vanishes exactly at box-constrained first-order stationary points.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(B\).

children.title: Bound-Face Stationarity Geometry
children.top_down_role: Stationarity structure induced by free, lower-active, and upper-active variable faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Face Stationarity Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise first-order conditions on the minimal box face containing a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(x\in[l,u]\). Define \(L(x)=\{i:x_i=l_i\}\), \(U(x)=\{i:x_i=u_i\}\), and \(F(x)=\{i:l_i<x_i<u_i\}\). Box stationarity is the coordinatewise predicate \(
abla_i q(x)\ge 0\) for \(i\in L(x)\), \(
abla_i q(x)\le 0\) for \(i\in U(x)\), and \(
abla_i q(x)=0\) for \(i\in F(x)\). Equivalently, the negative gradient belongs to \(N_{[l,u]}(x)\); on the relative interior of the current face, the gradient projected onto that face's tangent space is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary box point, free-coordinate gradients vanish, lower-bound gradients are nonnegative, and upper-bound gradients are nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate sign predicate is equivalent to \(0\in\nabla q(x)+N_{[l,u]}(x)\).

notation.meaning: indices active at lower and upper bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Projected Path Segments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-affine structure of a projected straight-line path through a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[l,u]\), \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), and define \(p(t)=P_{[l,u]}(x-td)\) for \(t\ge 0\). Each coordinate is \(p_i(t)=\min\{u_i,\max\{l_i,x_i-td_i\}\}\). Consequently, after sorting the finite bound-hitting times, \(p\) is affine on every open interval between consecutive distinct breakpoints. On such an interval, \(p_i'(t)=-d_i\) while coordinate \(i\) remains strictly between its bounds, and \(p_i'(t)=0\) after it is clipped at a bound. The path is continuous but generally nondifferentiable at breakpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected line through a box is continuous and piecewise affine; coordinates move linearly until they hit bounds and then remain clipped.
assumptions_latex: Projection is Euclidean and componentwise onto finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is continuous and piecewise affine, with slope changes only at bound-hitting times.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-Gradient Path: Criticality and Local Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-path characterization and descent properties for a quadratic over the infinity-norm trust-region box, with conditional convergence under a significant-step rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q\) be differentiable and let \(s\in[-\Delta,\Delta]^n\). For \(t\ge0\), define
\[
P(s,t)_i=\operatorname{mid}\{-\Delta,\ s_i-t[\nabla q(s)]_i,\ \Delta\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Then \(s\) is first-order critical for minimizing \(q\) over the box if and only if
\[
P(s,t)=s\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0.
\]
If \(s\) is not critical, there exists \(t_1>0\) such that
\[
q(P(s,t))<q(s)\qquad(0<t\le t_1).
\]
For the quadratic subproblem, repeatedly replacing \(s\) by \(P(s,t)\) converges to a first-order critical point when the selected steps are significant in the sense required by the convergence result; examples given are local minimization of the piecewise-quadratic path function or an Armijo-type backtracking search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected-gradient path clips a negative-gradient step to the trust-region box. Its fixed points for every nonnegative path parameter are exactly the first-order critical points. A noncritical point admits sufficiently short decreasing path steps, and the resulting iteration has the stated convergence only when a suitable significant-step rule is enforced.
assumptions_latex: q:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is differentiable; for the convergence claim, }q\text{ is the quadratic subproblem model}
\text{The convergence claim assumes a significant-step rule of the type stated in the source}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\text{ is first-order critical}\iff(\forall t\ge0)\,P(s,t)=s;\quad s\text{ noncritical}\implies(\exists t_1>0)(\forall t\in(0,t_1])\,q(P(s,t))<q(s),\text{ with convergence conditional on a significant-step rule.}

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Hitting Breakpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first hitting times along a projected box path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p(t)=P_{[l,u]}(x-td)\) with \(x\in[l,u]\), define the candidate hitting time of coordinate \(i\) by \(\tau_i=(x_i-l_i)/d_i\) when \(d_i>0\), \(\tau_i=(u_i-x_i)/(-d_i)\) when \(d_i<0\), and \(\tau_i=+\infty\) when \(d_i=0\). Retain finite nonnegative values, including zero for coordinates initially at the bound toward which they move. The distinct finite values among \(\{\tau_i\}\), ordered increasingly, are precisely the breakpoints where the affine formula for the projected path can change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each coordinate’s breakpoint is its distance to the bound approached by the path divided by its speed toward that bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite distinct \(\tau_i\) are exactly the possible slope-change times of \(P_{[l,u]}(x-td)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For coordinate hitting times \(\tau_i\), define \(E(\tau)=\{i:\tau_i=\tau\}\). A simultaneous breakpoint occurs at a finite \(\tau\ge 0\) precisely when \(|E(\tau)|\ge 2\). Every coordinate in \(E(\tau)\) is at its approached lower or upper bound at the event and is clipped on the path segment immediately to the right of \(\tau\). If \(\tau>0\) and coordinate \(i\in E(\tau)\) was moving freely immediately before the event, then \(p_i'(\tau^-)=-d_i\) and \(p_i'(\tau^+)=0\). At \(\tau=0\), only the right derivative is asserted. A breakpoint algorithm groups equal hitting times, according to exact equality or its declared numerical tolerance, and processes the entire group in one event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simultaneous event occurs when multiple coordinates share a finite hitting time; the whole group is clipped for the following path segment, while a left derivative is asserted only for positive-time events reached from a moving segment.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Cauchy-Point Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First projected-path minimizer for a box-constrained quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(z)=q(x)+g^{\mathsf T}(z-x)+\tfrac12(z-x)^{\mathsf T}H(z-x)\) on the box \(B=[l,u]\), where \(x\in B\) and \(g=\nabla q(x)\). Define the projected steepest-descent path \(p(t)=P_B(x-tg)\) for \(t\ge 0\). A generalized Cauchy point is \(x_C=p(t_C)\), where \(t_C\) is the smallest parameter at which \(q(p(t))\) attains a local minimum along this continuous piecewise-affine path; if the path becomes constant, its first constant point is admissible. Breakpoints partition the search into segments on which \(q(p(t))\) is a univariate quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized Cauchy point is the first local minimizer of the quadratic model along the box-projected negative-gradient path.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \(x\in[l,u]\), and all bounds are finite.
The projected path is searched in increasing \(t\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_C=P_B(x-t_Cg)\) is the first projected-path local minimizer under the stated convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Face Identification by Projected Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification under convergence and strict complementarity for projected-gradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^{k+1}=P_{[l,u]}(x^k-\alpha_k
abla q(x^k))\), where \(q\) has continuous gradient, \(x^k	o x^*\), and \(0<\underline\alpha\le\alpha_k\le\overline\alpha\). Suppose strict complementarity holds at \(x^*\): \(
abla_i q(x^*)>0\) whenever \(x_i^*=l_i\), and \(
abla_i q(x^*)<0\) whenever \(x_i^*=u_i\). Then there exists \(K\) such that, for every \(k\ge K\), each bound-active coordinate of \(x^*\) is projected onto the same bound in \(x^{k+1}\). Thus the strictly complementary active face is identified after finitely many projected-gradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent projected-gradient iterations identify every strictly complementary active bound after finitely many steps when step sizes stay uniformly positive and bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) has continuous gradient near \([l,u]\), and \(x^k\to x^*\).
Strict complementarity holds at every bound-active coordinate of \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is \(K\) such that all strictly complementary active bounds of \(x^*\) are correctly identified for every \(k\ge K\).

A primal-dual Newton correction satisfies \[\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}&0&-G^{\mathsf T}\\A&0&0&0\\G&0&-I&0\\0&0&Z&S\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta s\\\Delta z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_d\\-r_p\\-r_g\\r_c\end{bmatrix}.\] Choose a positive step length \(\alpha\) small enough that \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\) and \(z+\alpha\Delta z>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearizing dual stationarity, equality feasibility, slack feasibility, and centered complementarity produces the primal-dual QP Newton system, followed by a positivity-preserving step.
assumptions_latex: The QP is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(Gx-s=h\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\).
The current variables satisfy \(s\in\mathbb R^m_{++}\), \(z\in\mathbb R^m_{++}\), and \(y\in\mathbb R^p\).
The centering parameter satisfies \(\sigma\in[0,1]\), \(e\in\mathbb R^m\) is the all-ones vector, and \(\mu=s^{\mathsf T}z/m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block-system solution is the Newton correction for the stated primal-dual residual equations with the complementarity target \(Sz=\sigma\mu e\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices of inequality slacks and multipliers.
All-ones vector in the inequality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Condensed Interior-Point QP Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur condensation of slack and inequality-multiplier corrections from the primal-dual QP system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Eliminating \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta z\) from the full primal-dual Newton equations gives \[\begin{bmatrix}H+G^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}ZG&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_d+G^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}(r_c-Zr_g)\\-r_p\end{bmatrix}.\] Recover the eliminated directions using \(\Delta s=G\Delta x+r_g\) and \(\Delta z=S^{-1}(r_c-Z\Delta s)\), and then choose step lengths that preserve positivity of the slack and inequality-multiplier variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the slack and inequality-multiplier directions reduces the primal-dual equations to an augmented KKT system in the primal and equality-multiplier directions; the eliminated directions are then recovered algebraically.
assumptions_latex: The QP and primal-dual variables are those of the system with constraints \(Ax=b\) and \(Gx-s=h\), where \(s,z\in\mathbb R^m_{++}\).
The residuals are \(r_d=Hx+c+A^{\mathsf T}y-G^{\mathsf T}z\), \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_g=Gx-s-h\), and \(r_c=\sigma\mu e-Sz\).
The diagonal matrices are \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\) and \(Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\), so \(S\) is invertible.
The elimination is performed in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condensed system together with the recovery formulas is algebraically equivalent to the full primal-dual Newton system.

assumptions_latex: A polyhedral feasible set is \(P=\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\).
For \(x\in P\), the active index set is \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active face is degenerate exactly when its active constraint representation fails linear independence; multiplier representations may then be nonunique.

notation.meaning: Matrix having active constraint normals as rows.
Active constraint index set at the point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-representation degeneracy of an active polyhedral face, distinguished from curvature degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The active face containing \(x\) is constraint-degenerate when \[\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})<|I(x)|.\] Equivalently, there exists a nonzero vector \(\eta\in\mathbb R^{|I(x)|}\) such that \(A_{I(x)}^{\mathsf T}\eta=0\). For ordinary box constraints with \(\ell_i<u_i\), distinct active coordinate normals are independent; degeneracy can arise from redundant general inequalities or from coincident bounds such as \(\ell_i=u_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active face is constraint-degenerate when its active normals are linearly dependent, allowing redundant constraints and potentially nonunique multipliers.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Active Faces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank condition correctly characterizes linear dependence of the active constraint representation, but calling the geometric face itself degenerate is terminology-dependent and may also refer to multiplier or strict-complementarity degeneracy. A source fixing the intended convention is required.

children.title: Active-Set Chattering
children.top_down_role: Rapid repeated changes in predicted activity near degenerate or weakly active faces.

assumptions_latex: An active-set method generates feasible iterates \(x_k\) and active sets \(I_k\).
The iterates converge to a limit \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Chattering occurs when face identification fails to stabilize despite convergence of the primal iterates.

notation.meaning: Symmetric difference of two index sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic face-switching instability near a degenerate or weakly complementary QP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Active-set chattering is present when \(x_k\to x_*\) but the selected faces do not stabilize: for every \(K\) there exists \(k\ge K\) with \(I_{k+1}\triangle I_k\ne\varnothing\). A typical mechanism is a constraint with zero limiting slack and zero limiting multiplier, for which arbitrarily small numerical or model perturbations repeatedly change whether the constraint is declared active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chattering means iterates converge while constraints continue entering and leaving the active set indefinitely, commonly near weak complementarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Chattering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonstabilization condition is mathematically precise and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but the use of “chattering” and the asserted weak-complementarity mechanism require a method-specific authoritative source.

children.title: Working-Set Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated working-set configurations that prevent sustained solver progress.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic working-set method has state \((x_k,W_k)\).
No termination condition is satisfied on the repeated states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A repeated deterministic state implies that all subsequent states repeat periodically, so the algorithm cannot reach a new solution without a safeguard.

notation.meaning: Primal iterate associated with the working set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact periodic repetition of deterministic active-set solver states, stronger than ordinary chattering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Working-set cycling occurs if there exist integers \(j<k\) such that \((x_j,W_j)=(x_k,W_k)\), no stopping test holds, and the deterministic update rule makes the subsequent state sequence periodic. More generally, in finite precision the equality may be replaced by equality of the solver's stored state and pivot decisions. The cycle produces no strict progress in the objective or feasibility measure over one period.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycling is periodic repetition of the same deterministic working-set state without satisfying termination or making strict progress.
knowledge_statements.title: Working-Set Cycling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A repeated state implies periodic continuation only when the displayed pair is the complete state of a memoryless deterministic update rule. The record needs a source and an explicit convention covering tie-breaking, counters, and other stored solver state.

children.title: Anti-Cycling Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Selection and stabilization mechanisms intended to prevent repeated active-set patterns.

assumptions_latex: The solver has finitely many combinatorial working sets or bases.
Every nonterminal pivot strictly improves a prescribed lexicographic state key.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No working-set state can recur, and therefore the pivot sequence terminates after finitely many combinatorial states.

notation.meaning: Lexicographically ordered progress key for a solver state.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sufficient condition underlying lexicographic perturbation and deterministic anti-cycling rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An anti-cycling safeguard is sufficient if it assigns each admissible solver state a key \(\kappa(x,W)\) such that every nonterminal working-set change satisfies \[\kappa(x_{k+1},W_{k+1})\prec_{\mathrm{lex}}\kappa(x_k,W_k),\] and only finitely many keys are attainable. Lexicographic perturbation of degenerate constraints together with a fixed index tie-break is one implementation pattern; the perturbation must preserve the ordering until termination and be removed when reporting the unperturbed solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-state solver cannot cycle when deterministic tie-breaking forces a strict lexicographic improvement at every nonterminal pivot.
knowledge_statements.title: Anti-Cycling Safeguards

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Strict movement through a finite set of ordered keys is a valid abstract anti-cycling condition, but the claimed lexicographic-perturbation implementation and removal rule are method-specific and currently unsupported.

assumptions_latex: A face fixes active variables and leaves free coordinates \(x_F\).
The reduced Hessian \(H_{FF}\) has a vector \(d\ne0\) with \(d^{\mathsf T}H_{FF}d<0\).
The ray \(x_F+td\) remains feasible for all \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face-restricted QP is unbounded below along the feasible negative-curvature ray.

notation.meaning: Principal Hessian block on free variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative curvature in the free-variable restriction of an identified QP face.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Along the feasible ray, the restricted objective satisfies \[q_F(x_F+td)=q_F(x_F)+t\nabla q_F(x_F)^{\mathsf T}d+\tfrac12t^2d^{\mathsf T}H_{FF}d.\] Since \(d^{\mathsf T}H_{FF}d<0\), it follows that \(q_F(x_F+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). If bounds instead block the ray at finite \(t\), an unconstrained reduced Newton solve is invalid and the negative-curvature step must be truncated at a face boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative curvature makes an unbounded free-variable ray drive the quadratic to minus infinity; bounded rays require truncation at the face boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Free-Variable Subproblems

children.top_down_role: Optimality structure and exact or approximate solution families for quadratic minimization over trust regions.

assumptions_latex: The model Hessian satisfies \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euclidean-ball trust-region subproblem always has a global minimizer because its feasible set is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical possibly nonconvex quadratic model constrained by a Euclidean ball.

source_refs.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), and \(\Delta>0\), the Euclidean-ball trust-region subproblem is \[\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\;m(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|p\|_2\le\Delta.\] The matrix \(B\) need not be positive semidefinite. The feasible region is the closed Euclidean ball centered at the model origin, and any global solution is called a Euclidean trust-region step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a possibly nonconvex quadratic model over the closed Euclidean ball of prescribed radius centered at the current model point.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean-Ball Trust-Region Subproblems

source_witnesses.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: Diagonally Scaled Trust Regions
children.top_down_role: Trust-region geometries induced by variable-wise scaling metrics.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible region is an axis-aligned ellipsoid, and positive diagonal scaling converts it bijectively to a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned ellipsoidal geometry induced by a positive diagonal scaling.

source_refs.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A diagonally scaled trust-region subproblem is
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n} q(s):=g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|Ds\|_2\leq\Delta,
\]
where \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) and every \(d_i>0\). Its feasible set equals \(\{s:s^\top D^2s\leq\Delta^2\}\), an axis-aligned ellipsoid. Because \(D\) is nonsingular, the change of variables \(y=Ds\) maps this set bijectively onto \(\{y:\|y\|_2\leq\Delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal scaling defines an axis-aligned ellipsoidal trust region, which becomes a Euclidean ball after scaling the step coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonally Scaled Trust Regions

source_witnesses.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: General Ellipsoidal Trust Regions
children.top_down_role: Trust-region geometries induced by dense positive-definite metrics.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint \(s^\top Ms\leq\Delta^2\) defines a compact ellipsoid centered at the origin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin-centered ellipsoids generated by symmetric positive-definite metrics.

source_refs.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(M=M^\top\succ0\), the general ellipsoidal trust-region subproblem is
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n} q(s):=g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad s^\top Ms\leq\Delta^2.
\]
Equivalently, its constraint is \(\|s\|_M\leq\Delta\), where \(\|s\|_M:=\sqrt{s^\top Ms}\). Positive definiteness makes \(\|\cdot\|_M\) a norm and makes the feasible region bounded, closed, convex, and therefore compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite metric replaces the Euclidean ball by a compact, convex ellipsoid in which a quadratic model is minimized.
knowledge_statements.title: General Ellipsoidal Trust Regions

source_witnesses.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: Coordinate-Transformation Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence between ellipsoidal regions and spherical regions under suitable coordinate transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(M=M^\top\succ0\) belongs to \(\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and \(M^{1/2}\) denotes its symmetric positive-definite square root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ellipsoidal problem and the transformed Euclidean trust-region problem have identical objective values at corresponding points and exactly corresponding minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of a positive-definite ellipsoidal constraint to Euclidean geometry.

source_refs.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the bijection \(y=M^{1/2}s\), the problem
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n} g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad s^\top Ms\leq\Delta^2
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n} \widehat g^\top y+\tfrac12y^\top\widehat Hy
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|y\|_2\leq\Delta,
\]
where \(\widehat g=M^{-1/2}g\) and \(\widehat H=M^{-1/2}HM^{-1/2}\). The minimizers correspond exactly by \(s=M^{-1/2}y\), and corresponding points have equal objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the metric square root transforms an ellipsoidal trust-region problem exactly into a Euclidean trust-region problem with transformed gradient and Hessian, preserving objective values and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Transformation Equivalence

source_witnesses.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: Polyhedral Trust-Region Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Quadratic subproblems constrained by polyhedral trust-region shapes.

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(P=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:As\leq\mathbf 1_m\}\), where the inequality is componentwise.
\(P\) is bounded, full-dimensional, centrally symmetric, and contains the origin in its interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trust region \(\Delta P\) is a centrally symmetric polytope represented by the finitely many componentwise inequalities \(As\leq\Delta\mathbf 1_m\).

notation.meaning: Vector of ones in the inequality space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic minimization over a centrally symmetric polyhedral norm ball.

source_refs.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27
II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:As\leq\mathbf 1_m\}\) satisfy the stated assumptions, with the inequality interpreted componentwise, and define its Minkowski functional by
\[
\|s\|_P:=\inf\{t>0:s\in tP\}.
\]
A polyhedral trust-region subproblem is
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n} g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|s\|_P\leq\Delta.
\]
Its constraint is equivalently \(As\leq\Delta\mathbf 1_m\). Thus the feasible region is the scaled polytope \(\Delta P\), although the quadratic objective may remain nonconvex when \(H\not\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral trust-region subproblem minimizes a quadratic over a scaled centrally symmetric polytope, equivalently under finitely many componentwise linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Trust-Region Subproblems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27
II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: Shape-Changing Trust-Region Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Quadratic subproblems whose trust-region geometry varies across subspaces or iterations.

assumptions_latex: \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-r)}\) have orthonormal columns with \(UU^\top+VV^\top=I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hybrid norm produces a nonsmooth trust region whose shape depends on the selected orthogonal decomposition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specific hybrid max-norm version based on an orthogonal subspace decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the stated orthogonal decomposition, define
\[
\|s\|_{U,V}:=\max\{\|U^\top s\|_\infty,\|V^\top s\|_2\}.
\]
The associated shape-changing trust-region subproblem is
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n} g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|s\|_{U,V}\leq\Delta.
\]
Equivalently, both \(\|U^\top s\|_\infty\leq\Delta\) and \(\|V^\top s\|_2\leq\Delta\) hold. Changing \(U\) and \(V\), for example between iterations, changes the feasible geometry while preserving central symmetry and convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shape-changing trust region combines different norms on complementary subspaces, and its geometry changes when the selected subspaces change.
knowledge_statements.title: Shape-Changing Trust-Region Subproblems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed hybrid norm is mathematically coherent, but no citation establishes that this exact max combination is the intended shape-changing trust-region construction for this terminal container. A dedicated source is required before selecting among literature variants.

children.title: Nonsmooth Trust-Region Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Corners, facets, and other nonsmooth boundary features affecting trust-region solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|\) is a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Boundary stationarity must use a normal cone or norm subdifferential; a unique smooth outward normal need not exist.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone description at nonsmooth boundaries of finite-dimensional norm balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At any boundary point \(s\) with \(\|s\|=\Delta\), the normal cone of the norm ball satisfies
\[
N_{B_\Delta}(s)=\{\alpha z:\alpha\geq0,\ z\in\partial\|s\|\},
\qquad
\partial\|s\|=\{z:\|z\|_*=1,\ z^\top s=\|s\|\}.
\]
If \(\partial\|s\|\) contains more than one vector, the boundary has no unique supporting normal at \(s\). Consequently, first-order stationarity for a differentiable model \(q\) is \(0\in\nabla q(s)+N_{B_\Delta}(s)\), rather than a scalar multiplier times a uniquely defined boundary gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonsmooth norm-ball boundary, outward normals form a cone generated by norm subgradients, so stationarity is an inclusion rather than a smooth multiplier equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Trust-Region Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-cone and norm-subdifferential formulas are standard and internally consistent, but the record supplies no inspectable source for these nontrivial convex-analytic claims.

children.title: Diagonal-Metric Trust-Region Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Trust-region subproblems represented through independent coordinate scaling.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A diagonal metric yields the separable squared radius \(\sum_i d_i s_i^2\) and an equivalent coordinate-scaled Euclidean subproblem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable squared metric and its Euclidean coordinate representation.

source_refs.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The diagonal-metric subproblem
\[
\min_s g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad s^\top Ds=\sum_{i=1}^n d_i s_i^2\leq\Delta^2
\]
has a coordinate-separable squared metric. With \(y=D^{1/2}s\), it becomes
\[
\min_y (D^{-1/2}g)^\top y+\tfrac12y^\top(D^{-1/2}HD^{-1/2})y
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|y\|_2\leq\Delta.
\]
The map between feasible points and minimizers is the bijection \(s=D^{-1/2}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal metric separates the squared trust-region radius by coordinate and becomes Euclidean after componentwise rescaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal-Metric Trust-Region Subproblems

source_witnesses.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: Block-Diagonal-Metric Trust-Region Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Trust-region subproblems represented through structured metrics on variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block-diagonal metric is additively separable by block and reducible to a Euclidean ball by independent positive-definite block transformations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively separable metric geometry over a fixed coordinate-block partition.

source_refs.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(M=\operatorname{diag}(M_1,\ldots,M_k)\), the block-diagonal-metric trust-region subproblem is
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n} g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
s^\top Ms=\sum_{j=1}^k s_j^\top M_js_j\leq\Delta^2.
\]
Its squared metric radius is additive across blocks. Defining \(y_j=M_j^{1/2}s_j\) for every \(j\) transforms the constraint into
\[
\sum_{j=1}^k\|y_j\|_2^2\leq\Delta^2.
\]
This geometric separability does not require the objective Hessian \(H\) to be block diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal metric decomposes the squared trust-region radius into block contributions and becomes Euclidean under independent block transformations, though the quadratic objective may still couple different blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal-Metric Trust-Region Subproblems

source_witnesses.locator: II Trust-Region Methods for Unconstrained Optimization p. 113

children.title: Cross-Block Coupling Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits of block-diagonal representations when significant coupling crosses block partitions.

assumptions_latex: \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_k)\) follows a fixed nontrivial block partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Additive block separability of the quadratic metric holds exactly when every off-diagonal block of \(M\) vanishes.

notation.meaning: Metric block from block \(j\) to block \(i\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic boundary for separability under a prescribed block partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The metric expands as
\[
s^\top Ms=\sum_{i=1}^k s_i^\top M_{ii}s_i+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}s_i^\top M_{ij}s_j.
\]
It admits an additive representation \(s^\top Ms=\sum_{i=1}^k\phi_i(s_i)\) for all \(s\), with each \(\phi_i\) depending only on block \(i\), if and only if \(M_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i\neq j\). Thus any nonzero off-diagonal block creates a cross-block term and destroys separability of the trust-region constraint in the original block coordinates, even though a global linear coordinate transformation can still diagonalize \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric is separable over fixed blocks exactly when its off-diagonal blocks vanish; any nonzero cross-block term couples the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Coupling Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic boundary is plausible and the failure_boundary content kind fits the terminal container, but the exact if-and-only-if claim has no cited source. Source support is required for this nontrivial characterization.

children.title: Interior Trust-Region Solutions
children.top_down_role: Trust-region minimizers lying strictly inside the prescribed region.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An interior global solution exists exactly when an unconstrained global minimizer lies strictly inside the metric ball.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient condition for a global minimizer strictly inside an ellipsoidal trust region.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(s_*\) is an interior global solution of
\[
\min_s q(s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad s^\top Ms\leq\Delta^2
\]
if and only if
\[
Hs_*=-g,\qquad H\succeq0,\qquad s_*^\top Ms_*<\Delta^2.
\]
Equivalently, the trust-region multiplier is \(\lambda_*=0\), and \(s_*\) is an unconstrained global minimizer of \(q\) lying strictly inside the metric ball. If \(H\) is singular, this condition may hold for more than one \(s_*\); it requires \(-g\) to belong to the range of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior trust-region solution is precisely a feasible unconstrained global minimizer: the Hessian is positive semidefinite, stationarity holds, and the radius constraint is strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Trust-Region Solutions

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

children.title: Boundary Trust-Region Solutions
children.top_down_role: Trust-region minimizers lying on the active region boundary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed shifted-system, curvature, and active-radius conditions characterize boundary global minimizers of the ellipsoidal trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality characterization for solutions on an ellipsoidal trust-region boundary.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(s_*\) is a boundary global minimizer of
\[
\min_s q(s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad s^\top Ms\leq\Delta^2
\]
if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\geq0\) such that
\[
(H+\lambda_*M)s_*=-g,
\qquad H+\lambda_*M\succeq0,
\qquad s_*^\top Ms_*=\Delta^2.
\]
The multiplier can equal zero when an unconstrained minimizer lies exactly on the boundary. It must be positive whenever no unconstrained global minimizer is feasible and the active constraint supplies the curvature or displacement needed for global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary solution satisfies an active radius constraint and a positive-semidefinite shifted Hessian system for some nonnegative trust-region multiplier.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Trust-Region Solutions

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

children.title: Interior-to-Boundary Transitions
children.top_down_role: Changes in solution location as radius, gradient, or curvature conditions vary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When unconstrained global minimizers exist, their least metric norm is the exact threshold separating forced boundary solutions from possible interior solutions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius threshold governing interior versus boundary location for global trust-region solutions.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(H\succeq0\) and \(-g\in\operatorname{Range}(H)\). Define
\[
S_0:=\{s:Hs=-g\},
\qquad
\rho:=\min_{s\in S_0}\sqrt{s^\top Ms}.
\]
If \(0<\Delta<\rho\), every trust-region global minimizer lies on the boundary. If \(\Delta=\rho\), at least one unconstrained global minimizer first becomes feasible and lies on the boundary. If \(\Delta>\rho\), an interior global minimizer exists. If either \(H\not\succeq0\) or \(-g\notin\operatorname{Range}(H)\), the quadratic has no unconstrained global minimizer, and every finite-radius trust-region global minimizer is a boundary solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest metric norm of an unconstrained minimizer is the critical radius: below it solutions are forced to the boundary, while above it interior solutions exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior-to-Boundary Transitions

children.title: Shifted-Curvature Semidefinite Regimes
children.top_down_role: Trust-region settings classified by semidefiniteness of the multiplier-shifted quadratic curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Shifted-Curvature Semidefinite Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite curvature condition for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}q(x)\), where \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\). A feasible point \(x_*\) and scalar \(\lambda_*\) satisfy the shifted-curvature regime precisely when \[H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad (H+\lambda_*I)x_*=-g,\qquad \lambda_*\geq0,\qquad \lambda_*(\|x_*\|-\Delta)=0.\] These conditions are necessary and sufficient for \(x_*\) to be a global minimizer. In particular, semidefiniteness requires \(\lambda_*\geq\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is globally optimal exactly when a nonnegative shift makes the Hessian semidefinite, satisfies shifted stationarity, and obeys complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}q(x)\).

children.title: Positive Trust-Region Multipliers

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Trust-Region Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-boundary consequence of a strictly positive trust-region multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\), suppose \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfies the trust-region optimality conditions and \(\lambda_*>0\). Complementary slackness then gives \(\|x_*\|=\Delta\). If additionally \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\), then \[x_*=-(H+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g,\qquad \|(H+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\|=\Delta,\] and this boundary point is the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive multiplier forces the radius constraint active; a positive-definite shifted Hessian then yields the unique minimizer through the secular equation.
assumptions_latex: \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfies shifted stationarity, shifted semidefiniteness, feasibility, and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_*>0\Rightarrow\|x_*\|=\Delta\), with uniqueness when \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\).

children.title: Zero Trust-Region Multipliers
children.top_down_role: Inactive-boundary or limiting settings associated with a zero trust-region multiplier.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Trust-Region Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior or boundary solutions inherited from unconstrained convex quadratic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\), a trust-region optimality pair with \(\lambda_*=0\) exists exactly when \[H\succeq0,\qquad Hx_*=-g,\qquad \|x_*\|\leq\Delta.\] Thus \(x_*\) is also a global unconstrained minimizer of \(q\). Conversely, every feasible unconstrained minimizer gives a trust-region optimality pair \((x_*,0)\). If \(H\succ0\), the point is uniquely \(x_*=-H^{-1}g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero multiplier occurs precisely when a feasible unconstrained minimizer exists and the unshifted Hessian is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_*=0\) is valid exactly for feasible solutions of \(Hx_*=-g\) with \(H\succeq0\).

children.title: Singular Shift Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Multiplier values where shifted curvature becomes singular or changes spectral regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Shift Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard-case boundary where the shifted Hessian loses invertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda_b=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\). At the singular boundary \(H+\lambda_bI\succeq0\) and \(\det(H+\lambda_bI)=0\). Shifted stationarity is solvable only if \[g\in\operatorname{Range}(H+\lambda_bI),\] equivalently \(g\perp\ker(H+\lambda_bI)\). When solvable, every stationary point has the form \[x=x_p+z,\qquad x_p=-(H+\lambda_bI)^\dagger g,\qquad z\in\ker(H+\lambda_bI).\] Feasibility and complementarity must determine \(z\); inverse-based secular formulas fail at this boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a singular spectral shift, stationarity requires a range condition and leaves a nullspace component that feasibility must determine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((H+\lambda_bI)x=-g\) is solvable exactly when \(g\perp\ker(H+\lambda_bI)\).

children.title: Global Minimizer Certificates
children.top_down_role: Structural certificates distinguishing global trust-region minimizers from merely stationary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Minimizer Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient primal-multiplier certificate for global trust-region optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the subproblem \(\min_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\), a pair \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) is a verifiable global-minimizer certificate when \[\|x_*\|\leq\Delta,\quad \lambda_*\geq0,\quad (H+\lambda_*I)x_*=-g,\quad H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\quad \lambda_*(\|x_*\|^2-\Delta^2)=0.\] Such a certificate exists for every global minimizer, and any pair satisfying these displayed conditions certifies that \(x_*\) is globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility, shifted stationarity, shifted positive semidefiniteness, nonnegative multiplier, and complementarity form an exact global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}\bigl(\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\bigr)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted-Hessian and Complementarity Conditions for a Trust-Region Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary primal-dual conditions and a uniqueness criterion for the Euclidean-ball trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(s)=q_0+g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\), where \(H=H^\top\), and let \(\Delta>0\). If \(s^{\mathrm M}\) globally minimizes \(q\) subject to \(\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\), then there exists \(\lambda^{\mathrm M}\geq0\) such that \((H+\lambda^{\mathrm M}I)s^{\mathrm M}=-g\), \(H+\lambda^{\mathrm M}I\succeq0\), and \(\lambda^{\mathrm M}(\|s^{\mathrm M}\|_2-\Delta)=0\). If \(H+\lambda^{\mathrm M}I\succ0\), then \(s^{\mathrm M}\) is the unique global minimizer over the ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every global minimizer of a quadratic model over a Euclidean trust-region ball has a nonnegative multiplier satisfying shifted stationarity, positive-semidefinite shifted curvature, and trust-region complementarity. If the shifted Hessian is positive definite, the ball-constrained global minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda^{\mathrm M}\geq0:\ (H+\lambda^{\mathrm M}I)s^{\mathrm M}=-g,\quad H+\lambda^{\mathrm M}I\succeq0,\quad \lambda^{\mathrm M}(\|s^{\mathrm M}\|_2-\Delta)=0;\qquad H+\lambda^{\mathrm M}I\succ0\implies s^{\mathrm M}\text{ is the unique global minimizer on }\{s:\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted-Hessian Conditions for a Sphere-Constrained Quadratic Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary conditions and a uniqueness criterion for the equality-boundary Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(s)=q_0+g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\), where \(H=H^\top\), and let \(\Delta>0\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every global minimizer of a quadratic model on a Euclidean sphere satisfies a shifted stationarity equation with a positive-semidefinite shifted Hessian. If that shifted Hessian is positive definite, the sphere-constrained global minimizer is unique.

children.title: Unique Global Minimizers
children.top_down_role: Trust-region regimes admitting a single globally minimizing step.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Global Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness criterion expressed through the certified shifted system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\). Suppose \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfies \[\|x_*\|\leq\Delta,\quad \lambda_*\geq0,\quad (H+\lambda_*I)x_*=-g,\quad H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\quad \lambda_*(\|x_*\|^2-\Delta^2)=0.\] Set \(A_*=H+\lambda_*I\). If \(A_*\succ0\), then \(x_*=-A_*^{-1}g\) is the unique global minimizer. If \(A_*\) is singular, set \(x_p=-A_*^\dagger g\). In that case the global minimizer is unique exactly when \(\|x_p\|=\Delta\). Consequently, \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}q(x)\text{ is a singleton}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A_*\succ0\ \text{ or }\ \bigl(A_*\text{ is singular and }\|x_p\|=\Delta\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a certified trust-region multiplier, the global minimizer is unique exactly when the shifted Hessian is positive definite or its singular shifted system has a minimum-norm solution already on the trust-region boundary.
assumptions_latex: \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfies the displayed global trust-region certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}q(x)\) is a singleton exactly under the displayed criterion.

children.title: Multiple Global Minimizers
children.top_down_role: Trust-region regimes admitting distinct globally minimizing steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Global Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nullspace parametrization of all minimizers in the singular shifted regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\). Suppose \(\lambda_*\geq0\) is a global-certificate multiplier, so that \(A_*=H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\), \(g\in\operatorname{Range}(A_*)\), and some feasible solution of \(A_*x=-g\) satisfies complementarity. Assume \(A_*\) is singular, set \(x_p=-A_*^\dagger g\), and suppose \(\|x_p\|<\Delta\). If \(\lambda_*>0\), then all global minimizers are \[x_p+z,\qquad z\in\ker A_*,\qquad \|z\|^2=\Delta^2-\|x_p\|^2.\] If \(\lambda_*=0\), then all global minimizers are \[x_p+z,\qquad z\in\ker H,\qquad \|z\|^2\leq\Delta^2-\|x_p\|^2.\] In either case the minimizer set contains multiple points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a singular certified shift whose minimum-norm stationary solution lies strictly inside the ball, all global minimizers are its nullspace corrections. Positive multipliers require the residual norm to equal the remaining radius, while a zero multiplier permits any residual norm up to that radius.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_*\) is a global-certificate multiplier and \(A_*=H+\lambda_*I\) is singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}q(x)\) is exactly the applicable displayed nullspace family and is not a singleton.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Lagrangian Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-shift dual of the Euclidean trust-region quadratic subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p_* =\min_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}\bigl(\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\bigr)\), the Lagrangian dual is \[p_*=\max_{\lambda\geq0}\left\{-\tfrac12g^{\mathsf T}(H+\lambda I)^\dagger g-\tfrac12\lambda\Delta^2:\ H+\lambda I\succeq0,\ g\in\operatorname{Range}(H+\lambda I)\right\}.\] The equality is strong duality. Any maximizing \(\lambda_*\), together with a feasible solution of \((H+\lambda_*I)x=-g\) satisfying complementarity, recovers a primal global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trust-region value equals a one-dimensional concave dual maximization over nonnegative spectral shifts, including a range condition at singular shifts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_*\) equals the displayed dual optimum, with no duality gap.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar dual formula and recovery statement are standard and internally consistent, but strong duality and the singular-shift range condition have no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: S-Lemma Trust-Region Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: S-lemma certificate for a global lower bound on a ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(\Delta>0\). A scalar \(\gamma\) is a valid lower bound on the trust region, meaning \(q(x)\geq\gamma\) whenever \(\|x\|\leq\Delta\), if and only if there exists \(\lambda\geq0\) such that \[\begin{pmatrix}H+\lambda I&g\\g^{\mathsf T}&-2\gamma-\lambda\Delta^2\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] The strict feasibility point \(x=0\) for the ball supplies the Slater hypothesis required by the lossless S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic lower bound over the ball is valid exactly when one nonnegative multiplier makes the associated augmented matrix positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(\Delta>0\), so the ball constraint is strictly feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(x)\geq\gamma\) for all \(\|x\|\leq\Delta\) if and only if the displayed semidefinite certificate exists.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplier normalization and augmented matrix are mathematically consistent, and the ball has a Slater point, but the lossless S-lemma equivalence requires an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Trust-Region Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted semidefinite formulation of the trust-region value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trust-region value \(p_*\) has the exact lifted representation \[p_*=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\,X\in\mathbb S^n}\left\{\tfrac12\langle H,X\rangle+g^{\mathsf T}x:\ \operatorname{tr}(X)\leq\Delta^2,\ \begin{pmatrix}X&x\\x^{\mathsf T}&1\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] Although the constraint \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\) is relaxed to \(X\succeq xx^{\mathsf T}\), this semidefinite program has the same optimal value as the original trust-region subproblem and admits an optimal rank-one lift corresponding to a primal minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifting the quadratic to a semidefinite matrix gives an exact convex formulation, and an optimal rank-one lift recovers a trust-region minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed semidefinite program has value \(p_*\) and possesses an optimal solution with \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted SDP is the standard trust-region relaxation and the exactness claim is plausible, but equality of optimal values and existence of a rank-one optimum are nontrivial claims without cited evidence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global optimality conditions for the trust-region quadratic subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient characterization of global minimizers of a symmetric quadratic model over a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathbb R\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(B=B^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\). Then
\[
p^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|_2\leq\Delta}\left(f+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\right)
\]
if and only if \(\|p^*\|_2\leq\Delta\) and there exists \(\lambda\geq0\) such that
\[
(B+\lambda I)p^*=-g,\qquad \lambda(\Delta-\|p^*\|_2)=0,\qquad B+\lambda I\succeq0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible vector is a global minimizer of the trust-region quadratic model if and only if a nonnegative shift multiplier satisfies the shifted stationarity equation, complementarity with the trust-region boundary, and positive semidefiniteness of the shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|_2\leq\Delta}m(p)\iff\left[\|p^*\|_2\leq\Delta\ \land\ \exists\lambda\geq0:\ (B+\lambda I)p^*=-g,\ \lambda(\Delta-\|p^*\|_2)=0,\ B+\lambda I\succeq0\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue Trust-Region Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional maximum-eigenvalue representation of the trust-region value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[M(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12H&\tfrac12g\\[2pt]\tfrac12g^{\mathsf T}&t\end{pmatrix}.\] For \(p_* =\min_{\|x\|\leq\Delta}\bigl(\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x\bigr)\), one has the exact eigenvalue representation \[p_*=\max_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{(\Delta^2+1)\lambda_{\min}(M(t))-t\right\}.\] Thus the nonconvex quadratic subproblem is equivalent in optimal value to maximizing a concave scalar function formed from the smallest eigenvalue of an arrowhead matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trust-region optimum equals a scalar maximization involving the smallest eigenvalue of an augmented arrowhead matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_* =\max_{t\in\mathbb R}\bigl((\Delta^2+1)\lambda_{\min}(M(t))-t\bigr)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is not valid for the ball as stated. For n=1, H=2, g=0, and Delta=1, the trust-region value is 0, whereas the displayed maximization equals 1. The representation effectively enforces a boundary/sphere formulation unless an additional slack construction is introduced.

knowledge_statements.title: Shifted-Factorization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded Moré–Sorensen iteration in the positive-definite shifted regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(H\), \(g\), \(\Delta>0\), first accept \(x=-H^{-1}g\) with \(\lambda=0\) when \(H\succ0\) and \(\|x\|\leq\Delta\). Otherwise maintain a safeguarded interval above \(\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\). For each trial \(\lambda\), factor \(H+\lambda I=LL^{\mathsf T}\), solve \(x=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) and \(w=(H+\lambda I)^{-1}x\), and apply the safeguarded Newton update \[\lambda^+=\lambda-\frac{\|x\|^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}}{x^{\mathsf T}w/\|x\|^3}.\] Stop when the secular residual meets tolerance; handle a singular boundary by a nullspace correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated shifted factorizations and safeguarded Newton steps solve the secular equation; singular hard cases require a nullspace correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \((H+\lambda I)x=-g\) and either \(\lambda=0,\ \|x\|\leq\Delta\), or \(\lambda>0,\ \|x\|\approx\Delta\).

children.title: Trust-Region Multiplier Brackets
children.top_down_role: Lower and upper multiplier bounds used within nearly exact trust-region solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Multiplier Brackets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Easy-case bracket for the Euclidean trust-region secular equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem 
\[\min_{\|p\|\leq \Delta} g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp,\]
let \(\alpha=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\), \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\), and \(\phi(\lambda)=\|p(\lambda)\|^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}\) for \(\lambda>\alpha\). A valid multiplier bracket is a pair \(\lambda_L,\lambda_U\) satisfying \(\alpha\leq\lambda_L\leq\lambda_U\), positive definiteness wherever an inverse is evaluated, and
\[\phi(\lambda_L)\leq0\leq\phi(\lambda_U).\]
Because \(\phi\) is nondecreasing, every easy-case secular root \(\lambda_*\) lies in \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid bracket encloses the secular root between multipliers whose trial-step norms lie respectively above and below the trust-region radius.
assumptions_latex: The easy-case secular root exists with \(B+\lambda_*I\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_*\in[\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\).

children.title: Multiplier Safeguarding Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Controls that keep multiplier searches within numerically admissible spectral regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Safeguarding Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bracket-preserving safeguarded Newton iteration for the easy-case secular multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a valid bracket \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\) for the nondecreasing secular function \(\phi(\lambda)=\|p(\lambda)\|^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}\), where \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) and every evaluated shift is positive definite. At iteration \(k\), evaluate \(\phi(\lambda_k)\) and \(\phi'(\lambda_k)>0\), and form the Newton proposal \(\widehat\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k-\phi(\lambda_k)/\phi'(\lambda_k)\). If this proposal is outside a prescribed interior portion of \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\), or its shifted system is not sufficiently positive definite, replace it by a bracket-interior fallback such as bisection. After evaluating the accepted \(\lambda_{k+1}\), set \(\lambda_L\leftarrow\lambda_{k+1}\) when \(\phi(\lambda_{k+1})\leq0\), and set \(\lambda_U\leftarrow\lambda_{k+1}\) otherwise. Stop when the bracket width or secular residual meets its prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safeguarded Newton proposals are kept inside a sign-changing multiplier bracket and the positive-definite evaluation domain, with bisection or another bracket-interior step used when a proposal is unsafe.
assumptions_latex: \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\) is a valid easy-case multiplier bracket.
\(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) are evaluable at every accepted iterate, with \(\phi'(\lambda)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updated interval remains a valid bracket containing \(\lambda_*\).
