children.title: Near-Singular Bracket Behavior
children.top_down_role: Bracket sensitivity near singular shifted systems or hard-case spectral values.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Singular Bracket Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavior at the spectral boundary separating easy and hard trust-region cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), \(E_1=\ker(B-\theta_1I)\), \(\alpha=-\theta_1\), and \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) for \(\lambda>\alpha\). If the orthogonal projection of \(g\) onto \(E_1\) is nonzero, then \[\|p(\lambda)\|\to\infty\quad\text{and}\quad \|p(\lambda)\|^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}\to-\Delta^{-1}\qquad\text{as }\lambda\downarrow\alpha.\] If that projection is zero, then \(p(\lambda)\to p_0=-(B+\alpha I)^\dagger g\). When \(\|p_0\|\leq\Delta\), the singular hard-case solution has the form \[p_*=p_0+z,\qquad z\in E_1,\qquad \|p_*\|=\Delta.\] If instead \(\|p_0\|>\Delta\), the boundary equation has an easy-case root strictly above \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero gradient component in the critical eigenspace makes the easy-case step norm diverge at the spectral boundary. With an orthogonal gradient, hard-case augmentation is required only when the limiting pseudoinverse step has norm no larger than the trust-region radius.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), so the singular multiplier boundary is \(\alpha=-\lambda_{\min}(B)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of \(g\) onto \(E_1\), together with the norm of \(-(B+\alpha I)^\dagger g\), distinguishes divergence, an easy root above the boundary, and hard-case augmentation.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Secular Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense spectral solution of the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute an orthogonal eigendecomposition \(B=Q\operatorname{diag}(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)Q^{\mathsf T}\), with \(\theta_1\leq\cdots\leq\theta_n\), and set \(c=Q^{\mathsf T}g\). If \(B\succeq0\) and there is a feasible vector \(p_0\) satisfying \(Bp_0=-g\), return such a \(p_0\). Otherwise, in the positive-definite easy case solve \[\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{c_i^2}{(\theta_i+\lambda)^2}=\Delta^2\] over multipliers satisfying \(\lambda\geq0\) and \(\theta_i+\lambda>0\) for every \(i\), then set \(y_i=-c_i/(\theta_i+\lambda)\) and \(p=Qy\). At a singular hard-case multiplier \(\lambda=-\theta_1\geq0\), use the pseudoinverse components for the positive denominators and add a vector in the minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace so that \(\|p\|=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonalizing the Hessian converts the boundary condition into a scalar rational equation and permits direct reconstruction of easy- and hard-case trust-region steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed \(p\), together with its multiplier \(\lambda\), satisfies the trust-region global-optimality conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization-Based Secular Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Easy-case secular iteration using shifted Cholesky factorizations without eigendecomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\), define \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) and \(\phi(\lambda)=\|p(\lambda)\|^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}\) on the positive-definite shift domain. For a bracketed iterate \(\lambda_k\) with \(A_k=B+\lambda_kI\succ0\), form \(A_k=R_k^{\mathsf T}R_k\), solve \(A_kp_k=-g\), and solve \(R_k^{\mathsf T}q_k=p_k\). Evaluate \[\phi'(\lambda_k)=\frac{\|q_k\|^2}{\|p_k\|^3}.\] Propose \(\widehat\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k-\phi(\lambda_k)/\phi'(\lambda_k)\), safeguard the proposal within the current multiplier bracket and positive-definite domain, refactor, and update the bracket according to the sign of \(\phi\). Stop when the norm residual and shifted-system residual satisfy their prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shifted Cholesky solves provide both the trial step and the secular derivative, enabling safeguarded Newton updates without an eigendecomposition.
assumptions_latex: The desired solution lies in the positive-definite easy case.
A valid initial multiplier bracket is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the returned \((p_k,\lambda_k)\) satisfies the prescribed boundary and shifted-system residual tolerances.

notation.meaning: Cholesky factor of the shifted Hessian
auxiliary vector used to evaluate the secular derivative

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Generalized-Eigenvalue TRS Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense block-eigenvalue method for an easy-case Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Form the dense block matrix
\[\mathcal M=\begin{pmatrix}-B&gg^{\mathsf T}/\Delta^2\\ I&-B\end{pmatrix}.\]
Compute its rightmost real eigenvalue \(\lambda_*\). When \(B+lambda_*I\succ0\), solve \((B+lambda_*I)p_*=-g\), normalize only to remove roundoff-level boundary error, and verify \(\|p_*\|=\Delta\). The characteristic relation
\[\det\!\left((B+lambda I)^2-gg^{\mathsf T}/\Delta^2\right)=0\]
contains the secular equation for a boundary solution. Accept the returned pair only after checking stationarity, feasibility, and positive semidefiniteness of the shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense block eigenproblem yields a candidate trust-region multiplier, from which the boundary step is recovered and certified.
assumptions_latex: The global solution is a boundary easy-case solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A verified rightmost eigenpair yields \((p_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfying the trust-region optimality conditions.

notation.meaning: dense block matrix encoding the secular equation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the specialized block matrix, rightmost-eigenvalue selection, or recovery claim. Several multiplier occurrences are also malformed; mathematical and source verification must precede revision.

knowledge_statements.title: Large Sparse Generalized-Eigenvalue TRS Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free Krylov realization of the block-eigenvalue trust-region formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent the block operator by
\[\mathcal M\binom{u}{v}=\binom{-Bu+g(g^{\mathsf T}v)/\Delta^2}{u-Bv},\]
without forming \(\mathcal M\). Apply an implicitly restarted Arnoldi or rational Krylov method targeting the rightmost real eigenpair \((\lambda,w)\). Recover \(prom(B+lambda I)p=-g\) using a sparse shifted solver. Continue or enlarge the Krylov space until the eigenresidual, stationarity residual, boundary residual, and a lower-bound estimate for \(\lambda_{
min}(B+lambda I)\) meet prescribed tolerances. Return \((p,lambda)\) only if these certificate checks pass; otherwise report an unresolved or hard-case subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free Krylov eigensolver targets the rightmost eigenvalue of the block operator, followed by sparse recovery and certification of the step.
assumptions_latex: Products with \(B\), inner products with \(g\), and shifted linear solves are available.
The targeted eigenvalue is sufficiently isolated for the chosen Krylov method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Passing all residual and curvature tests produces a nearly exact sparse trust-region solution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrix-free generalized-eigenvalue algorithm lacks any citation, and the recovery equation contains corrupted text (`prom`) and a broken minimum-eigenvalue command. Its precise algorithm and certificates require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Generalized-Eigenvalue TRS Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of an ellipsoidal trust region to the Euclidean eigenvalue formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[\min_{p^{\mathsf T}Mp\leq\Delta^2}g^{\mathsf T}p+tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp,\qquad M\succ0.\]
With \(y=M^{1/2}p\), define \(H=M^{-1/2}BM^{-1/2}\) and \(h=M^{-1/2}g\). The problem is equivalent to
\[\min_{\|y\|\leq\Delta}h^{\mathsf T}y+tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}Hy.\]
A Euclidean generalized-eigenvalue TRS solver applied to \((H,h,Delta)\) returns \(y_*\) and multiplier \(\lambda_*\); then \(p_*=M^{-1/2}y_*\), and the original stationarity equation is \((B+lambda_*M)p_*=-g\). Implementations may use factorizations of \(M\) instead of explicit square roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite metric transforms an ellipsoidal trust region into a Euclidean one; the recovered step satisfies a metric-shifted stationarity equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_*=M^{-1/2}y_*\) solves the ellipsoidal subproblem whenever \(y_*\) solves the transformed Euclidean subproblem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric transformation is plausible, but no source supports its placement as a generalized-eigenvalue solver, while the record is only a representation rather than a solver algorithm. Several formulas also contain malformed commands.

children.title: Exact Trust-Region Solver Regime
children.top_down_role: Solver use cases requiring a globally optimal trust-region solution to the prescribed numerical standard.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Trust-Region Solver Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient global-optimality certificate for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp,\qquad \|p\|\leq\Delta,\] a feasible vector \(p_*\) is a global minimizer if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\geq0\) such that \[(B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda_*(\|p_*\|-\Delta)=0.\] Thus an exact solver returns \((p_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfying these relations in its stated arithmetic model. The certificate covers interior solutions, boundary easy cases, and singular hard cases. In particular, \(p_*\) is unique when \(B+\lambda_*I\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step and nonnegative multiplier solve the trust-region problem exactly if and only if stationarity, complementary slackness, and positive semidefiniteness of the shifted Hessian hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditions are necessary and sufficient for global optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Exact Trust-Region Solver Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based acceptance conditions for a numerically nearly exact Euclidean trust-region solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g,p\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\). Given nonnegative tolerances \(\varepsilon_s,\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_\lambda,\varepsilon_H,\varepsilon_c\), accept \((p,\lambda)\) as nearly exact only if \[\|p\|\leq\Delta+\varepsilon_f,\qquad \lambda\geq-\varepsilon_\lambda,\qquad \|(B+\lambda I)p+g\|\leq\varepsilon_s,\] \[\lambda_{\min}(B+\lambda I)\geq-\varepsilon_H,\qquad |\lambda(\|p\|-\Delta)|\leq\varepsilon_c.\] The tolerances must be scaled consistently with the problem data and arithmetic precision. A small secular residual alone is insufficient, particularly near a singular hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearly exact pair is accepted only when it jointly passes scaled feasibility, multiplier-sign, stationarity, shifted-curvature, and complementarity tests.
assumptions_latex: \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g,p\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\).
All five tolerances are nonnegative and use a stated scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((p,\lambda)\) is accepted under this convention only when every displayed test holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Cauchy-Point Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization of the quadratic trust-region model along the negative-gradient ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\). For \(g\neq0\), restrict the model to \(p=-tg\) with \(0\leq t\leq\Delta/\|g\|\), and define \[t_C=\begin{cases}\min\!\left\{\dfrac{\|g\|^2}{g^{\mathsf T}Bg},\dfrac{\Delta}{\|g\|}\right\},&g^{\mathsf T}Bg>0,\\[6pt]\dfrac{\Delta}{\|g\|},&g^{\mathsf T}Bg\leq0,\end{cases}\qquad p_C=-t_Cg.\] If \(g=0\), set \(p_C=0\). For \(g\neq0\), the point \(p_C\) minimizes \(q(-tg)\) over the feasible negative-gradient segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cauchy point exactly minimizes the quadratic model along the feasible negative-gradient segment, truncating at the boundary when curvature is nonpositive or the line minimizer is too long.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(g\neq0\), \(p_C\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p=-tg,\ 0\leq t\leq\Delta/\|g\|}q(p)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenpoint Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional trust-region minimization along a signed approximate minimum-eigenvector direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\). Choose a unit vector \(u\) approximating a minimum-eigenvalue eigenvector of \(B\), and reverse its sign if necessary so that \(g^{\mathsf T}u\leq0\). Set \(a=g^{\mathsf T}u\) and \(\kappa=u^{\mathsf T}Bu\). The minimizer of \(q(tu)=at+\tfrac12\kappa t^2\) over \(0\leq t\leq\Delta\) is given by \[t_E=\begin{cases}\min\{\Delta,-a/\kappa\},&\kappa>0,\\ \Delta,&\kappa\leq0,\end{cases}\qquad p_E=t_Eu.\] The resulting eigenpoint supplies trial-point decrease associated with the selected curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An eigenpoint minimizes the quadratic model along a signed approximate minimum-eigenvector direction, moving to the boundary whenever the directional curvature is nonpositive.
assumptions_latex: The sign of \(u\) is selected so that \(g^{\mathsf T}u\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_E\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq t\leq\Delta}q(tu)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dogleg and Double-Dogleg Trust-Region Step Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-linear approximate solution of a quadratic trust-region subproblem using Cauchy and Newton-oriented reference points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k^C\) be the Cauchy step and \(s_k^N=-B_k^{-1}g_k\) the Newton or quasi-Newton step. If \(\lVert s_k^N\rVert\leq\Delta_k\), choose \(s_k=s_k^N\). Otherwise, the classical dogleg construction chooses the intersection of \(\lVert s\rVert=\Delta_k\) with the path \(0\to s_k^C\to s_k^N\). The double-dogleg construction inserts a point \(\widehat N\) on the Newton direction and uses the path \(0\to s_k^C\to\widehat N\to s_k^N\), choosing its applicable boundary intersection. In either case, \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the Newton or quasi-Newton step lies inside the trust region, it is used directly. Otherwise, classical dogleg selects the trust-region-boundary intersection of the path from the origin through the Cauchy step toward the Newton step. Double dogleg inserts an additional Newton-direction point to bias the path toward that direction.
assumptions_latex: s_k^N=-B_k^{-1}g_k\text{ is a defined Newton or quasi-Newton step.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_k=\begin{cases}s_k^N,&\lVert s_k^N\rVert\leq\Delta_k,\\ \text{a boundary intersection of the selected dogleg path},&\lVert s_k^N\rVert>\Delta_k,\end{cases}\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical two-segment dogleg construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of the classical dogleg approximation for a positive-definite quadratic trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(p)=f+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), where \(B\succ0\), \(g\ne0\), and \(p^{\mathrm B}=-B^{-1}g\). The exact trust-region solution is approximately \(-\Delta g/\|g\|\) for small \(\Delta\) and generally traces a curved trajectory as the radius varies. The classical dogleg method replaces that trajectory by \[p^{\mathrm U}=-\frac{g^Tg}{g^TBg}g,\qquad \widetilde p(\tau)=\begin{cases}\tau p^{\mathrm U},&0\le\tau\le1,\\p^{\mathrm U}+(\tau-1)(p^{\mathrm B}-p^{\mathrm U}),&1\le\tau\le2.\end{cases}\] It selects a point minimizing \(m\) over the portion of this path satisfying \(\|p\|\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite quadratic model, the classical dogleg path runs from the origin to the steepest-descent line minimizer and then to the unconstrained quadratic minimizer. The dogleg step minimizes the model over the feasible part of this two-segment path, which approximates the curved exact-solution trajectory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{\mathrm D}=\widetilde p(\tau_*),\qquad \tau_*\in\arg\min_{\substack{0\le\tau\le2\\\|\widetilde p(\tau)\|\le\Delta}}m(\widetilde p(\tau)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaled Double-Dogleg Trust-Region Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate quadratic trust-region solver selecting the radius intersection of a piecewise-linear path through steepest-descent and Newton-oriented points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For H=LL^T\succ0, s_N=-H^{-1}g, and D=\operatorname{diag}(S), approximately solve \min_s\ g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs subject to \|Ds\|_2\le\delta. If \|Ds_N\|_2\le\delta, return s=s_N and set \delta=\|Ds_N\|_2. Otherwise construct the double-dogleg path through 0, the scaled Cauchy step s_{SD}, \eta s_N, and s_N, where 0<\eta\le1, and return the unique point s on the path satisfying \|Ds\|_2=\delta. Depending on the radius, this point lies on the scaled steepest-descent segment, the segment from s_{SD} to \eta s_N, or the Newton-direction segment from \eta s_N to s_N.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take the Newton step when it lies inside the trust region. Otherwise construct the double-dogleg path through the Cauchy step and an intermediate multiple of the Newton step, then return the unique point where the appropriate path segment meets the scaled trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s=s_N\text{ if }\|Ds_N\|_2\le\delta;\text{ otherwise }s\text{ lies on the double-dogleg path and }\|Ds\|_2=\delta.

knowledge_statements.title: Dogleg Path Selection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise norm conditions governing endpoint acceptance and the first boundary interpolation on a radially ordered dogleg path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\|v_m\|\le\Delta\), select \(v_m\). Otherwise let \(i\) be the smallest index satisfying \(\|v_i\|<\Delta\le\|v_{i+1}\|\), set \(d_i=v_{i+1}-v_i\), and select \(v_i+\tau_i d_i\), where \(\tau_i\in(0,1]\) is the unique admissible root of \[\|d_i\|^2\tau^2+2v_i^{\mathsf T}d_i\tau+\|v_i\|^2-\Delta^2=0.\] If some vertex satisfies \(\|v_i\|=\Delta\), that vertex is the first boundary point when all preceding vertices have norm strictly below \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a path whose vertex norms are nondecreasing, accept the feasible terminal vertex; otherwise find the first inside-to-outside segment and solve its scalar boundary-intersection equation.
assumptions_latex: A polygonal dogleg path has ordered vertices \(v_0=0,v_1,\ldots,v_m\) in a Euclidean space, and \(\Delta>0\).
The vertex norms are radially ordered: \(\|v_0\|\le\|v_1\|\le\cdots\le\|v_m\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditions select either the feasible terminal vertex or the unique first intersection of the path with \(\{p:\|p\|=\Delta\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m(p)=f+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\) with \(B\succ0\), the unconstrained minimizer is \(p^B=-B^{-1}g\). If \(p^*(\Delta)\in\arg\min_{\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta}m(p)\) and \(\Delta\geq\lVert p^B\rVert\), then \(p^*(\Delta)=p^B\). The classical dogleg method is presented for this positive-definite regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a positive-definite model matrix, the full Newton-type step uniquely minimizes the unconstrained quadratic model. Whenever the trust-region radius is at least the norm of that step, it is feasible and is also the trust-region solution. This is the applicability regime used to motivate classical dogleg.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact trust-region minimization after restriction to a chosen subspace of dimension one or two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct an orthonormal basis matrix \(Z\) for \(S=\operatorname{span}\{u,v\}\), and define \(\widehat g=Z^{\mathsf T}g\) and \(\widehat H=Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\). Compute \[y_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|y\|\le\Delta}\left(\widehat g^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}\widehat Hy\right)\] using an exact one- or two-dimensional trust-region solver, and return \(s_*=Zy_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the quadratic onto a one- or two-dimensional subspace, solve the reduced trust-region problem exactly, and lift a reduced minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The vectors \(u\) and \(v\) span a subspace \(S\) of dimension one or two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned point \(s_*\) belongs to \(S\), satisfies \(\|s_*\|\le\Delta\), and minimizes \(q\) over \(S\cap\{s:\|s\|\le\Delta\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-dimensional trust-region subspace minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted quadratic trust-region minimization in a gradient-curvature subspace, together with the extraction's partial outline for indefinite and singular curvature cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m(p)=f+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), \(B\succ0\), and \(\Delta>0\), compute \[p_{2D}\in\arg\min\{m(p):\|p\|\le\Delta,\ p\in\operatorname{span}[g,B^{-1}g]\}.\] This is a two-variable problem and can be reduced algebraically to finding the roots of a quartic polynomial. The restricted feasible set contains the Cauchy point and the entire classical dogleg path; hence \(m(p_{2D})\le m(p^{\mathrm c})\), so the method supplies at least Cauchy model reduction. When embedded in a trust-region framework whose standard global-convergence hypotheses make Cauchy decrease sufficient, it preserves that convergence mechanism. If \(B\) has most negative eigenvalue \(\lambda_1<0\), the stated variant uses \[\operatorname{span}[g,(B+\alpha I)^{-1}g],\qquad \alpha\in(-\lambda_1,-2\lambda_1],\] for which \(B+\alpha I\succ0\). Writing \(s=(B+\alpha I)^{-1}g\), when \(\|s\|\le\Delta\) the extraction instead specifies \(p=-s+v\) with \(v^Ts\le0\); this orientation condition ensures \(\|p\|\ge\|s\|\), but the extract explicitly leaves the remaining choice of \(v\) to the detailed method. If \(B\succeq0\) is singular and has no negative eigenvalues, the stated fallback is \(p=p^{\mathrm c}\). When \(B=\nabla^2f(x_k)\) is positive definite near a solution and \(\Delta\) is sufficiently large, the restricted minimizer is the Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method minimizes the quadratic trust-region model over the span of the gradient and Newton direction. Because this subspace contains both the Cauchy point and the dogleg path, its solution achieves at least Cauchy reduction and extends dogleg. The extraction also outlines a shifted subspace for indefinite curvature and a Cauchy-point fallback for positive-semidefinite singular curvature, but does not fully specify the auxiliary vector used by the indefinite variant. With a positive-definite exact Hessian near a solution and a sufficiently large radius, the method selects the Newton step.
assumptions_latex: B\succ0\text{ for the unshifted two-dimensional method}
\lambda_1<0\text{ is the most negative eigenvalue in the indefinite case}
\text{Any global-convergence conclusion additionally requires the usual surrounding trust-region assumptions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{2D}\in\arg\min_{\substack{\|p\|\le\Delta\\p\in\operatorname{span}[g,B^{-1}g]}}m(p),\qquad m(p_{2D})\le m(p^{\mathrm c})\quad(B\succ0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: CG–Steihaug Trust-Region Subproblem Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic trust-region subproblem addressed by CG–Steihaug and its use within an outer trust-region method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $\Delta_k>0$ and $B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)$, CG--Steihaug computes an approximate solution of $$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}m_k(p):=f_k+\nabla f_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp\quad\text{subject to }\|p\|\leq\Delta_k.$$ The method is designed to provide an improvement on the Cauchy-point approximation. A complete trust-region minimization method uses the resulting $p_k$ as the trial step of the outer trust-region algorithm, with an inner tolerance $\epsilon_k$ selected at each major iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CG–Steihaug approximately solves the quadratic trust-region subproblem and is designed to improve on the Cauchy-point approximation. Its output supplies the trial step for an outer trust-region method, with an inner tolerance chosen at each iteration.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon_k>0\text{ is selected for the inner iteration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k\text{ is an approximate trust-region-subproblem solution that can be used as the outer trust-region trial step.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: CG–Steihaug Truncated Conjugate-Gradient Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual, nonpositive-curvature, trust-region-boundary, and accuracy termination rules for a quadratic trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $\epsilon_k>0$, set $z_0=0$, $r_0=\nabla f_k$, and $d_0=-r_0$. If $\|r_0\|<\epsilon_k$, return $p_k=0$. Otherwise, for $j=0,1,\ldots$: if $d_j^TB_kd_j\leq0$, choose $\tau$ so that $p_k=z_j+\tau d_j$ lies on $\|p_k\|=\Delta_k$ and minimizes $m_k$ over the boundary intersections of that line, then return $p_k$. If $d_j^TB_kd_j>0$, set $a_j=(r_j^Tr_j)/(d_j^TB_kd_j)$ and $z_{j+1}=z_j+a_jd_j$. If $\|z_{j+1}\|\geq\Delta_k$, choose $\tau\geq0$ so that $p_k=z_j+\tau d_j$ and $\|p_k\|=\Delta_k$, then return $p_k$. Otherwise set $r_{j+1}=r_j+a_jB_kd_j$; if $\|r_{j+1}\|<\epsilon_k$, return $p_k=z_{j+1}$. If not, set $\beta_{j+1}=(r_{j+1}^Tr_{j+1})/(r_j^Tr_j)$ and $d_{j+1}=-r_{j+1}+\beta_{j+1}d_j$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start CG at the zero step and return zero if the initial residual is already small. On nonpositive curvature, move along the current CG line to the boundary intersection having the smaller model value. If an ordinary CG step reaches or crosses the trust-region boundary, truncate the segment at the boundary. Otherwise continue until the residual tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k\text{ is returned upon residual convergence, detection of nonpositive curvature, or first contact with }\|p\|=\Delta_k.}

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steihaug–Toint termination when the current CG direction has nonpositive curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p_k^{\mathsf T}Hp_k\le0\), compute the unique \(\tau_*>0\) satisfying \(\|s_k+\tau_*p_k\|=\Delta\), return \(s_*=s_k+\tau_*p_k\), and terminate the truncated-CG iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a descending CG direction has nonpositive curvature, move along it to the trust-region boundary and terminate.
assumptions_latex: \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\), where \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\), and the trust region has radius \(\Delta>0\).
At iterate \(s_k\), the direction \(p_k\ne0\) satisfies \(\|s_k\|<\Delta\) and \(\nabla q(s_k)^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(s_k+\tau_*p_k\) is feasible, lies on the trust-region boundary, and minimizes \(q(s_k+\tau p_k)\) over the feasible forward interval \(\tau\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Boundary Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steihaug–Toint truncation when a positive-curvature CG step exits the trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose the smallest \(\tau_k\in(0,\alpha_k]\) satisfying \[\|s_k+\tau_kp_k\|=\Delta.\] Equivalently, \(\tau_k\) is the admissible positive root of \[\|p_k\|^2\tau^2+2s_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\tau+\|s_k\|^2-\Delta^2=0.\] Return \(s_*=s_k+\tau_kp_k\) and terminate. If the full step lies on the boundary, then \(\tau_k=\alpha_k\); otherwise \(0<\tau_k<\alpha_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the next CG iterate would leave the trust region, shorten that step to its first boundary intersection and terminate.
assumptions_latex: A CG iterate \(s_k\) satisfies \(\|s_k\|<\Delta\), its search direction is \(p_k\ne0\), and its proposed positive-curvature step length is \(\alpha_k>0\).
The full step reaches or crosses the trust-region boundary: \(\|s_k+\alpha_kp_k\|\ge\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned point \(s_*=s_k+\tau_kp_k\) is the first boundary point encountered by the proposed CG step.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(s_0=0\), \(r_0=g\), \(z_0=M^{-1}r_0\), and \(p_0=-z_0\). At iteration \(k\), if \(p_k^{\mathsf T}Hp_k\le0\), return the forward \(M\)-norm boundary intersection. Otherwise set \(\alpha_k=(r_k^{\mathsf T}z_k)/(p_k^{\mathsf T}Hp_k)\). If \(s_k+\alpha_kp_k\) reaches or crosses the boundary, return its first boundary intersection. Else update \(s_{k+1}=s_k+\alpha_kp_k\), \(r_{k+1}=r_k+\alpha_kHp_k\), \(z_{k+1}=M^{-1}r_{k+1}\), \(\beta_{k+1}=(r_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}z_{k+1})/(r_k^{\mathsf T}z_k)\), and \(p_{k+1}=-z_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}p_k\); stop when the prescribed residual tolerance holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run preconditioned CG in the preconditioner norm, stopping at residual tolerance, nonpositive curvature, or the trust-region boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose the first Lanczos vector \(q_1=g/\|g\|\), so that \(Q_k^{\mathsf T}g=\|g\|e_1\). Every \(s\in\mathcal K_k(H,g)\) has the form \(s=Q_ky\), with \(\|s\|=\|y\|\), and \[q(Q_ky)=\|g\|e_1^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}T_ky.\] Consequently, minimizing \(q\) over \(\mathcal K_k(H,g)\cap\{s:\|s\|\le\Delta\}\) is equivalent to the reduced trust-region subproblem \[\min_{\|y\|\le\Delta}\ \|g\|e_1^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}T_ky.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal Lanczos basis converts the trust-region problem restricted to a Krylov space into a smaller tridiagonal trust-region problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Truncated Lanczos Trust-Region Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Increasing-dimensional Lanczos projection with exact reduced solves and a prescribed truncation test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize Lanczos with \(q_1=g/\|g\|\). For \(k=1,2,\ldots\), extend \(Q_k\), form \(T_k=Q_k^{\mathsf T}HQ_k\), and solve \[y_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|y\|\le\Delta}\left(\|g\|e_1^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}T_ky\right).\] Set \(s_k=Q_ky_k\). Stop when a prescribed projected-optimality tolerance, model-decrease tolerance, iteration limit, or Lanczos-breakdown criterion is met, and return the last \(s_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expand a Lanczos basis, solve each tridiagonal reduced trust-region problem, and return the lifted solution when a specified truncation criterion holds.
assumptions_latex: Lanczos iterations can compute Hessian-vector products and maintain an orthonormal basis for \(\mathcal K_k(H,g)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(s_k\) is feasible and minimizes \(q\) over \(\mathcal K_k(H,g)\cap\{s:\|s\|\le\Delta\}\); the algorithm returns the minimizer associated with its final generated Krylov subspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: GLTR expressed through symmetric preconditioning and exact reduced trust-region solves for a nonzero starting gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Apply Lanczos to \(\widetilde H=M^{-1/2}HM^{-1/2}\) starting from \(\widetilde g=M^{-1/2}g\), obtaining an orthonormal basis \(Q_k\) and \(T_k=Q_k^{\mathsf T}\widetilde HQ_k\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The active-boundary subproblem is in the easy spectral regime when \(P_{E_1}g\ne0\). Then there exists a unique multiplier \(\sigma_*>\max\{0,-\lambda_1\}\) satisfying the secular equation \[\left\|(H+\sigma_*I)^{-1}g\right\|=\Delta.\] The unique global minimizer is \(s_*=-(H+\sigma_*I)^{-1}g\), and it satisfies \((H+\sigma_*I)s_*=-g\), \(H+\sigma_*I\succ0\), and \(\|s_*\|=\Delta\). The strict inequality excludes the singular shift responsible for the hard spectral regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the gradient has a component in the leftmost eigenspace, a unique nonsingular shift solves the secular equation and yields the boundary minimizer.

children.top_down_role: Trust-region cases characterized by deficient gradient coupling with the critical eigenspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard Spectral Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Euclidean trust-region hard case, including boundary completion in the minimum eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem is in the hard spectral regime when \(\lambda_1<0\), \(g\perp E_1\), and \(\|(H-\lambda_1I)^\dagger g\|_2\leq\Delta\). Equivalently, the limiting positive-semidefinite shift \(H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\) is singular at \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_1\), while the stationarity equation \((H+\lambda_*I)x=-g\) is consistent. Every global solution has the form \(x_* = -(H-\lambda_1I)^\dagger g+z\), where \(z\in E_1\) and \(\|x_*\|_2=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard regime occurs when the gradient is orthogonal to the minimum eigenspace and the singular shifted system has a pseudoinverse solution inside or on the trust-region boundary; a possibly zero minimum-eigenspace component completes it to the boundary.
assumptions_latex: The trust-region problem has objective \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Hx+g^\top x\) and constraint \(\|x\|_2\leq\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_* = -(H-\lambda_1 I)^\dagger g+z\) for some \(z\in E_1\) chosen so that \(\|x_*\|_2=\Delta\), and the optimal multiplier is \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_1\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the symmetric Hessian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Model-Value Bound for a Boundary-Reaching Low-Curvature Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard-regime approximation certificate for a corrected quadratic trust-region step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\lambda\in\mathcal G\), \(s(\lambda)=-H(\lambda)^{-1}g\), and, for some \(\kappa_{\mathrm{hard}}\in(0,1)\), the vector \(v\) satisfies \[\langle v,H(\lambda)v\rangle\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{hard}}\left(\langle s(\lambda),H(\lambda)s(\lambda)\rangle+\lambda\Delta^2\right),\qquad \|s(\lambda)+v\|_2=\Delta.\] Then \[q\bigl(s(\lambda)+v\bigr)\leq(1-\kappa_{\mathrm{hard}})q(s^{\mathrm M}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the correction reaches the trust-region boundary and satisfies the stated shifted-curvature bound, the corrected step obeys the given model-value approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\bigl(s(\lambda)+v\bigr)\leq(1-\kappa_{\mathrm{hard}})q(s^{\mathrm M})

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Hard Spectral Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic transition from the easy regime as the leftmost-eigenspace gradient component vanishes toward hard-case data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), a boundary solution of \((H+\lambda I)x=-g_\varepsilon\) with \(H+\lambda I\succ0\) satisfies \(\lambda>-\lambda_1\) and \(\|(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g_\varepsilon\|_2=\Delta\). Its minimum-eigenspace component has norm \(\varepsilon/(\lambda+\lambda_1)\). If \(g_\varepsilon\to g_0\), \(P_1g_0=0\), and \(\|(H-\lambda_1I)^\dagger g_0\|_2<\Delta\), then the corresponding multipliers approach \(-\lambda_1\); hence the shifted systems become nearly singular and the easy-regime solutions approach minimum-eigenspace completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When easy-regime data approach hard-case data satisfying the completion condition, the multiplier approaches the singular endpoint and the shifted systems become increasingly ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \(\Delta>0\), and the smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) is separated from the remaining spectrum by a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the boundary-solution multiplier approaches \(-\lambda_1\), and the shifted system approaches singularity.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto the minimum eigenspace of H
Magnitude of the varying gradient component in the minimum eigenspace

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: solvability and solution-set formula for a symmetric singular linear system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic structure of the singular stationarity system at the hard-case shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the endpoint shift, \(M=H+\lambda I\succeq0\) is singular. The trust-region stationarity system \(Mx=-g\) is consistent if and only if \(g\in\operatorname{range}(M)\), equivalently \(g\perp E\). When consistent, its complete solution set is \(x=-M^\dagger g+z\) with \(z\in E\). If \(g\not\perp E\), no solution exists at the singular shift, and a feasible KKT multiplier must lie strictly above \(-\lambda_{\min}(H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the endpoint shift, stationarity is solvable precisely when the gradient is orthogonal to the nullspace; every solution then equals a pseudoinverse solution plus a null vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Shifted TRS Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-system solvability and pseudoinverse description are standard and fit the node, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any \(z\in\ker M\) with \(\|z\|_2=\sqrt{\Delta^2-\|x_0\|_2^2}\) yields the global solution \(x_*=x_0+z\).

notation.meaning: Minimum-norm solution of the singular stationarity system
Minimum eigenspace, equal to the nullspace of M

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical minimum-eigenspace completion for the trust-region hard case
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary completion after solving the consistent singular shifted system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \(x_0=-M^\dagger g\). Choose any unit vector \(u\in E=\ker M\), set \(\tau=\sqrt{\Delta^2-\|x_0\|_2^2}\), and output \(x_*=x_0+\tau u\). Since \(x_0\in\operatorname{range}(M)=E^\perp\), one has \(\|x_*\|_2=\Delta\). More generally, every \(z\in E\) with \(\|z\|_2=\tau\) gives a completed solution; if \(\tau=0\), output \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve with the pseudoinverse, then add a minimum-eigenvector component of exactly the length needed to reach the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Eigenspace Completion Mechanisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The completion algorithm is internally consistent and correctly uses orthogonality of the pseudoinverse solution and nullspace, but it lacks an authoritative source with an exact locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Hard-Case Numerical Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order spectral sensitivity near a simple smallest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Writing \(\alpha=u_1^\top g\) and \(\delta=\lambda+\lambda_1>0\), the minimum-eigenvector component is \(u_1^\top x(\lambda)=-\alpha/\delta\). Perturbations \((d\alpha,d\delta)\) therefore satisfy \[d(u_1^\top x)=-\frac{d\alpha}{\delta}+\frac{\alpha\,d\delta}{\delta^2}.\] Thus absolute errors in the gradient projection or multiplier can produce large absolute solution errors as \(\delta\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the hard case, division by the small shifted eigenvalue strongly amplifies absolute errors in the gradient projection and computed multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb S^n\) has a simple smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) with unit eigenvector \(u_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The component \(u_1^\top x(\lambda)=-(u_1^\top g)/(\lambda+\lambda_1)\) has absolute sensitivity that grows as \(\lambda+\lambda_1\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Distance of the shift from singularity
Gradient component along the minimum eigenvector

knowledge_statements.title: Single Indefinite-Quadratic-Constraint GTRS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inequality-form GTRS with one indefinite quadratic constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single indefinite-quadratic-constraint generalized trust-region subproblem is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n} q_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_1(x)\leq0,\] where \(q_0(x)=x^\top Ax+2a^\top x+\alpha\) and \(q_1(x)=x^\top Bx+2b^\top x+\beta\), and \(B\) has both positive and negative eigenvalues. Consequently, the feasible set need not be convex. The model has exactly one quadratic inequality; additional affine constraints are not included in this local definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This GTRS minimizes one quadratic function subject to one quadratic inequality whose Hessian is indefinite, so the feasible set can be nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\), and \(B\) has both positive and negative eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The GTRS is \(\inf\{x^\top Ax+2a^\top x+\alpha:q_1(x)\leq0\}\), where \(q_1(x)=x^\top Bx+2b^\top x+\beta\) has an indefinite quadratic part.

knowledge_statements.title: GTRS Lagrangian Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Lagrangian duality for the inequality-form GTRS under strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q_0(x)=x^\top Ax+2a^\top x+\alpha\) and \(q_1(x)=x^\top Bx+2b^\top x+\beta\), strict feasibility and finite primal value imply \[\inf_{q_1(x)\leq0}q_0(x)=\sup_{\lambda\geq0}\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda).\] Equivalently, the common value is \[\sup_{\lambda\geq0,\gamma\in\mathbb R}\left\{\gamma:\begin{pmatrix}A+\lambda B&a+\lambda b\\(a+\lambda b)^\top&\alpha+\lambda\beta-\gamma\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] Hence the duality gap is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility and finite value, the GTRS equals its scalar-multiplier Lagrangian dual, which admits a semidefinite matrix formulation.
assumptions_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(q_1(\bar x)<0\).
The primal GTRS has a finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal value equals \(\sup_{\lambda\geq0}\inf_x\{q_0(x)+\lambda q_1(x)\}\), equivalently the stated semidefinite dual value.

notation.meaning: Lagrangian multiplier for the quadratic inequality

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rank-one exactness of the standard lifted relaxation for one quadratic inequality under regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Shor lifting for an attained, strictly feasible single-constraint GTRS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lifted relaxation is \[\inf_{x,X}\ A\bullet X+2a^\top x+\alpha\quad\text{subject to}\quad B\bullet X+2b^\top x+\beta\leq0,\quad\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Under the stated regularity assumptions, its value equals the GTRS value. Moreover, an optimal lifted solution can be selected with \(X=xx^\top\), so that the moment matrix has rank one and \(x\) is a globally optimal GTRS point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With strict feasibility and attainment, the standard lifted SDP for one quadratic constraint is value-exact and has a rank-one optimal solution recoverable as a GTRS optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact GTRS Semidefinite Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and rank-one recovery claim fit the leaf and are coherent under value exactness plus attained primal optimum, but the exact hypotheses and S-lemma/SDP-exactness claim need an authoritative theorem-level citation.

children.title: GTRS SDP-Exactness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural settings where semidefinite exactness becomes delicate or ceases to hold.

assumptions_latex: Consider the standard lifted relaxation of a quadratic program with one quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a strict feasible point, or after adding further quadratic constraints, zero duality gap and rank-one recoverability are not guaranteed by the single-constraint S-lemma.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scope boundary of the strict S-lemma and single-constraint SDP exactness theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the standard exactness guarantee, not a claim that every degenerate instance has a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The usual GTRS exactness argument requires a strict-feasibility condition such as the existence of \(\bar x\) with \(q_1(\bar x)<0\), together with finiteness and the relevant attainment conditions. If strict feasibility is removed, the strict S-lemma cannot be invoked in that form; if independent quadratic constraints are added, a single scalar multiplier no longer describes their joint implication. Therefore neither zero Lagrangian duality gap nor existence of an optimal lift satisfying \(X=xx^\top\) follows from the standard single-constraint theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard exactness guarantee ends when strict feasibility fails or multiple independent quadratic constraints replace the single constraint; exactness may still hold instance by instance.
knowledge_statements.title: GTRS SDP-Exactness Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement carefully limits itself to the boundary of the standard guarantee rather than asserting universal failure, but the boundary claim lacks a source and no concrete gap example is cited.

assumptions_latex: The number of quadratic constraints is part of the input dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General QCQP with multiple quadratic constraints is NP-hard; the polynomially tractable single-constraint GTRS theory therefore does not extend unrestrictedly.

notation.meaning: Binary sign variables in the reduction
Symmetric matrix encoding a binary quadratic objective

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: binary quadratic optimization embeds into QCQP using quadratic sign constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case boundary when the number of quadratic constraints grows with the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Binary quadratic optimization embeds into a multiple-constraint QCQP by imposing, for each \(i\), the two inequalities \(x_i^2-1\leq0\) and \(1-x_i^2\leq0\), which together enforce \(x_i^2=1\). Thus minimizing \(x^\top Wx\) over \(x_i\in\{-1,1\}\) is a QCQP with \(m=2n\) quadratic inequalities. Since this family contains NP-hard binary quadratic problems, unrestricted QCQP with an input-dependent number of quadratic constraints is NP-hard; the tractability mechanism specific to one quadratic constraint cannot extend generally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing a growing number of quadratic constraints captures binary quadratic optimization through sign-enforcing constraints, making the unrestricted problem class NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Quadratic-Constraint Tractability Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign-constraint embedding is explicit and the complexity-bound kind fits the tractability-boundary leaf, but the NP-hard source problem and reduction require an authoritative complexity citation with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT matrix representation for an equality-constrained quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian stationarity system and block-inverse formulas for an equality-constrained quadratic program; invertibility guarantees a unique stationary pair, not by itself an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the equality-constrained quadratic program
\[
\min_x\;\tfrac12x^{\mathrm T}Gx+g^{\mathrm T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad A^{\mathrm T}x=b,
\]
with Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=\tfrac12x^{\mathrm T}Gx+g^{\mathrm T}x-\lambda^{\mathrm T}(A^{\mathrm T}x-b)\), the stationarity equations can be written as
\[
K\binom{x}{\lambda}=-\binom{g}{b},\qquad K=\begin{bmatrix}G&-A\\-A^{\mathrm T}&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
When \(G=G^{\mathrm T}\), \(K\) is symmetric; if the multiplier block has positive dimension, \(K\) is not positive definite. If
\[
K^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}H&-T\\-T^{\mathrm T}&U\end{bmatrix},
\]
then the unique solution of the stationarity system is
\[
x^*=-Hg+Tb,\qquad \lambda^*=T^{\mathrm T}g-Ub.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangian stationarity conditions for an equality-constrained quadratic program form a symmetric KKT linear system. With at least one multiplier, its zero multiplier diagonal block prevents positive definiteness. If the KKT matrix is invertible and its inverse is partitioned into blocks H, T, and U, the unique stationary pair is x* = -Hg + Tb and lambda* = T^T g - Ub. Invertibility alone does not establish that this pair is an optimizer.
assumptions_latex: A^{\mathrm T}x=b\text{ is the equality-constraint system}
K=\begin{bmatrix}G&-A\\-A^{\mathrm T}&0\end{bmatrix}\text{ is invertible for the block-inverse formulas}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\binom{x^*}{\lambda^*}=-\binom{g}{b},\qquad x^*=-Hg+Tb,\quad \lambda^*=T^{\mathrm T}g-Ub.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT system and solvability alternatives for equality-constrained convex quadratic minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers convex quadratic objectives with affine equality constraints, including nonsingular, singular-consistent, and inconsistent KKT systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \min_x\{\tfrac12x^TPx+q^Tx+r:Ax=b\}, where P\in\mathbb{S}_+^n and A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}, the KKT conditions are \begin{bmatrix}P&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x^\star\\\nu^\star\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-q\\b\end{bmatrix}. If the KKT matrix is nonsingular, this system has a unique optimal primal-dual pair. If it is singular but the system is solvable, every solution is an optimal primal-dual pair. If the system is inconsistent, the quadratic program is infeasible or unbounded below. In the inconsistent case there exist v\in\mathbb{R}^n and w\in\mathbb{R}^p satisfying Pv+A^Tw=0, Av=0, and -q^Tv+b^Tw>0; if a feasible point \widehat{x} exists, then \widehat{x}+tv is feasible and f(\widehat{x}+tv)\to-\infty as t\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimality conditions for an equality-constrained convex quadratic program form a block linear KKT system. A nonsingular KKT matrix yields a unique optimal primal-dual pair, while every solution of a singular but consistent system is also optimal. If the system is inconsistent, the problem is infeasible or unbounded below; when the constraints are feasible, the displayed null direction certifies unbounded descent along a feasible ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\begin{bmatrix}x^\star\\\nu^\star\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-q\\b\end{bmatrix},\quad K=\begin{bmatrix}P&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix};\quad K\text{ nonsingular}\Rightarrow\text{a unique optimal pair};\quad Kz=d\text{ singular and solvable}\Rightarrow\text{every solution is optimal};\quad Kz=d\text{ inconsistent}\Rightarrow\text{infeasible or unbounded below}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent nonsingularity criteria for an equality-constrained convex-QP KKT matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes KKT-matrix nonsingularity through common nullspaces and positive definiteness on feasible directions, assuming positive-semidefinite quadratic curvature and a full-row-rank equality matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P\in\mathbb{S}_+^n and A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n} with \operatorname{rank}A=p<n, and define K=\begin{bmatrix}P&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}. Then the following are equivalent: K is nonsingular; \mathcal{N}(P)\cap\mathcal{N}(A)=\{0\}; Ax=0 and x\ne0 imply x^TPx>0; and F^TPF\succ0 for any F\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-p)} satisfying \mathcal{R}(F)=\mathcal{N}(A). In particular, P\succ0 implies that K is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-semidefinite quadratic Hessian and a full-row-rank equality matrix, the KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the Hessian and constraint matrix have no nonzero common null vector. Equivalently, the Hessian is positive definite on the constraint nullspace, or its null-space reduced matrix is positive definite. A positive-definite full Hessian is a sufficient special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ nonsingular}\iff \mathcal{N}(P)\cap\mathcal{N}(A)=\{0\}\iff \bigl(Ax=0,\ x\ne0\Rightarrow x^TPx>0\bigr)\iff F^TPF\succ0;\qquad P\succ0\Rightarrow K\text{ nonsingular}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse of a positive-definite saddle-point matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingularity criterion and Schur-complement inverse formula for a KKT matrix with a positive-definite primal block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be positive definite, $V\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&V^T\\V&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $M$ is invertible if and only if $V$ has full row rank. When $\operatorname{rank}(V)=m$, the matrix $VA^{-1}V^T$ is invertible and \[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{-1}-A^{-1}V^T(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}VA^{-1}&A^{-1}V^T(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}\\(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}VA^{-1}&-(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KKT saddle-point matrix with a positive-definite leading block is nonsingular exactly when the constraint matrix has linearly independent rows. Under that condition, its inverse is given by the displayed Schur-complement formula.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\text{ is positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is invertible}\iff\operatorname{rank}(V)=m;\quad \operatorname{rank}(V)=m\Rightarrow M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{-1}-A^{-1}V^T(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}VA^{-1}&A^{-1}V^T(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}\\(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}VA^{-1}&-(VA^{-1}V^T)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaled primal-dual Newton/KKT system for a convex quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slack-form Newton-system representation used in CVXMOD's Mehrotra predictor-corrector implementation. The reported block reduction is implementation-specific; the extract gives no convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x \tfrac12x^TPx+q^Tx\) subject to \(Gx\le h\) and \(Ax=b\), with \(P\succeq0\). Introduce \(s\ge0\) by \(Gx+s=h\), inequality multipliers \(z\ge0\), equality multipliers \(y\), and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(z)\). The KKT equations are \(Px+q+G^Tz+A^Ty=0\), \(Gx+s=h\), \(Ax=b\), and \(ZS=0\). At an interior-point iterate with \(s,z>0\), their Newton linearization has coefficient matrix \[\begin{bmatrix}P&0&G^T&A^T\\0&Z&S&0\\G&I&0&0\\A&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}.\] Scaling the complementarity row by \(S^{-1}\) yields \[\begin{bmatrix}P&0&G^T&A^T\\0&S^{-1}Z&I&0\\G&I&0&0\\A&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta s\\\Delta z\\\Delta y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_1\\S^{-1}r_2\\r_3\\r_4\end{bmatrix}.\] CVXMOD applies two block-elimination steps to obtain a reduced \(2\times2\) block KKT system, and a Mehrotra predictor-corrector iteration solves the coefficient system with two right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex QP, introducing nonnegative slacks gives primal-dual KKT equations. At an iterate with strictly positive slack and inequality-dual variables, scaling the linearized complementarity row by the inverse slack matrix produces a symmetric KKT-form Newton system. CVXMOD reduces this system by two block eliminations and uses two right-hand sides for the Mehrotra predictor and corrector computations. No convergence guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{bmatrix}P&0&G^T&A^T\\0&S^{-1}Z&I&0\\G&I&0&0\\A&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta s\\\Delta z\\\Delta y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_1\\S^{-1}r_2\\r_3\\r_4\end{bmatrix},\quad\text{with a reported two-step block reduction to a }2\times2\text{ block KKT system.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invertibility Criterion for the Equality-Constrained Least-Squares KKT Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient rank conditions for nonsingularity of the equality-constrained least-squares KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\). Then
\[
K=\begin{bmatrix}2A^{T}A&C^{T}\\ C&0\end{bmatrix}
\]
is invertible if and only if \(C\) has full row rank and \(\begin{bmatrix}A\\C\end{bmatrix}\) has full column rank. Equivalently, \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=p\) and \(\ker(A)\cap\ker(C)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The equality-constrained least-squares KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the rows of C are linearly independent and A and C have no common nonzero null vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{bmatrix}2A^{T}A&C^{T}\\ C&0\end{bmatrix}\text{ is invertible}\iff \operatorname{rank}(C)=p\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}\!\begin{bmatrix}A\\C\end{bmatrix}=n.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Saddle-Point Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unregularized equality-constrained QP KKT matrix in primal-dual block form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linearized stationarity and feasibility equations are \(Hp+A^\top y=-r_d\) and \(Ap=-r_p\). Their canonical saddle-point representation is \[\begin{pmatrix}H&A^\top\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p\\y\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}r_d\\r_p\end{pmatrix}.\] The coefficient matrix is symmetric. If \(m>0\), \(A\) has full row rank, and \(H\) is positive definite on \(\ker A\), the KKT matrix is nonsingular and indefinite, and the correction is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical KKT representation couples stationarity and feasibility in a symmetric saddle-point matrix. Under full row rank and positive definiteness of the Hessian on the constraint nullspace, the matrix is nonsingular and indefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and the equality-constrained QP is \(\min_x\tfrac12x^\top Hx+c^\top x\) subject to \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A primal-dual KKT correction solves \(\begin{pmatrix}H&A^\top\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p\\y\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}r_d\\r_p\end{pmatrix}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical KKT System for an Equality-Constrained Quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric saddle-point representation of stationarity and equality feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q(x)=g^Tx+\tfrac12x^TGx\) subject to \(A^Tx=b\), a pair \((x,\lambda)\) satisfies the KKT stationarity and feasibility equations exactly when \[\begin{bmatrix}G&-A\\-A^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\\lambda\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}g\\b\end{bmatrix}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stationarity and equality-feasibility equations for an equality-constrained quadratic form a canonical symmetric saddle-point linear system.

children.top_down_role: Reduced KKT systems formed by eliminating selected primal or dual blocks.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating \(z\) yields an equivalent augmented KKT system with primal block \(H+G^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}G\).

notation.meaning: Primal, equality-multiplier, and eliminable auxiliary increments

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}&G^{\mathsf T}\\A&0&0\\G&0&-W\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_x\\r_y\\r_z\end{bmatrix},\qquad W\succ0.\] The third block equation gives \(z=W^{-1}(Gx-r_z)\). Substitution produces the equivalent condensed KKT representation \[\begin{bmatrix}M&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_x+G^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}r_z\\r_y\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=H+G^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}G.\] After solving it, the eliminated variable is recovered from the displayed formula for \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating an auxiliary block with positive-definite weight produces an equivalent two-by-two KKT system and an explicit recovery formula.

children.title: Normal-Equation Representations
children.top_down_role: Reduced systems represented through normal-equation structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT system is equivalent to the positive-definite normal equation \((AM^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})y=AM^{-1}r_x-r_y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual normal equations obtained from a positive-definite condensed KKT system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the condensed KKT equations \[Mx+A^{\mathsf T}y=r_x,\qquad Ax=r_y,\] assume \(M\succ0\) and that \(A\) has full row rank. Eliminating \(x=M^{-1}(r_x-A^{\mathsf T}y)\) gives \[Ny=AM^{-1}r_x-r_y,\qquad N=AM^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}.\] The normal-equation matrix satisfies \(N\succ0\), so the dual solution is unique; the primal solution is recovered by the elimination formula. Thus the normal equation and the original condensed KKT system have the same solution pair \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating primal variables from a positive-definite KKT system gives positive-definite dual normal equations, followed by primal recovery.

children.title: Condensation Conditioning Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Sparsity and numerical-conditioning consequences of condensed or normal-equation forms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(AM^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})=\kappa_2(B)^2\), although condensation reduces system dimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral conditioning cost of forming dual normal equations.

source_refs.locator: 4.3.3 Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\succ0\), let \(A\) have full row rank, and set \(B=AM^{-1/2}\). The dual normal-equation matrix is \[N=AM^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}=BB^{\mathsf T}.\] Consequently, \[\kappa_2(N)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(B)^2}{\sigma_{\min}(B)^2}=\kappa_2(B)^2.\] Condensation replaces a larger indefinite KKT system by a smaller positive-definite system, but it can square the relevant spectral condition number and may create fill in \(N\). Therefore reduced dimension and compatibility with positive-definite solvers must be weighed against conditioning and sparsity loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal-equation condensation reduces dimension and yields positive definiteness, but can square conditioning and increase fill.
knowledge_statements.title: Condensation Conditioning Tradeoffs

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stationarity on the feasible affine space is equivalent to \((Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)u=-Z^{\mathsf T}(Hp_0+g)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: null-space parameterization of equality-constrained quadratic programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Null-space reduction for equality-constrained quadratic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \frac12p^{\mathsf T}Hp+g^{\mathsf T}p\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ap=b,\] let \(A\) have full row rank, choose \(p_0\) with \(Ap_0=b\), and let the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) form a basis of \(\ker A\). Every feasible point is uniquely \(p=p_0+Zu\). Stationarity over the feasible affine space is therefore equivalent to \[(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)u=-Z^{\mathsf T}(Hp_0+g).\] If \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\succ0\), this reduced system has a unique solution and the corresponding \(p\) is the unique constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A null-space basis parameterizes all feasible steps and reduces the equality-constrained QP to a system involving the reduced Hessian.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Hessian Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The null-space reduction and uniqueness conclusion are standard and fit a representation record, but no source is cited. The statement should also explicitly introduce H in S^n, g in R^n, and b in R^m rather than leaving their domains implicit.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-KKT solve by symmetric indefinite factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct solution of a symmetric indefinite KKT system using a permuted block LDL-transpose factorization, including the loss-of-sparsity cost boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonsingular symmetric indefinite KKT system \(Kx=b\), compute \[P^TKP=LBL^T,\] where \(P\) is a permutation matrix, \(L\) is unit lower triangular, and \(B\) is block diagonal with \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) blocks. Solve successively \[Lz=P^Tb,\qquad B\widehat z=z,\qquad L^T\bar z=\widehat z,\qquad x=P\bar z.\] For \(b=\begin{bmatrix}g\\h\end{bmatrix}\), this gives \(x=\begin{bmatrix}-p\\\lambda^*\end{bmatrix}\). Symmetric permutations are selected for numerical stability and, for sparse systems, to limit fill. The method can become expensive when the ordering fails to preserve sparsity and \(L\) becomes substantially denser than \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor the full symmetric indefinite KKT matrix using a permuted block LDL-transpose factorization, perform two triangular solves and one block-diagonal solve, and undo the permutation. The method may become expensive when ordering fails to control fill in the triangular factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x=PL^{-T}B^{-1}L^{-1}P^Tb\quad\text{satisfies}\quad Kx=b.

assumptions_latex: At each nonterminal step, the pivoting rule selects a nonsingular symmetric \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) principal block of the active Schur complement
The process either eliminates all indices or reports failure or singularity
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If all indices are eliminated, the algorithm returns \(P^{\mathsf T}KP=LDL^{\mathsf T}\); otherwise it reports that the prescribed pivoting rule did not complete the factorization.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{n}\), repeatedly apply a symmetric interchange that places a selected nonsingular \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) principal pivot block of the active Schur complement in pivot position, compute the associated multipliers, and update the trailing Schur complement symmetrically. A stability-oriented selection rule accepts only pivots satisfying its prescribed bound and reports failure or singularity if it cannot select a required pivot. If all indices are eliminated, the output satisfies \[P^{\mathsf T}KP=LDL^{\mathsf T},\] where \(P\) is a permutation matrix, \(L\) is unit lower triangular, and \(D\) is symmetric block diagonal with \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) pivot blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric-indefinite pivoting uses symmetric interchanges and acceptable one-by-one or two-by-two pivots; if elimination completes, it produces a permuted block LDL factorization, and otherwise it reports failure or singularity.

children.title: Static Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Predetermined or structurally fixed pivot choices for sparse indefinite KKT factorizations.

assumptions_latex: A symmetric ordering and pivot sequence are fixed before numeric elimination
Every prescribed pivot block is nonsingular
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm follows the predetermined symbolic structure, but stability is conditional on the prescribed pivots remaining numerically acceptable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: static pivoting fixes the numeric pivot sequence from symbolic information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predetermined pivot sequence for sparse symmetric-indefinite factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{n}\), choose a symmetric permutation \(P\) and a sequence of \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) pivot blocks before numerical factorization. Numeric elimination then follows that sequence without data-dependent interchanges and returns \[P^{\mathsf T}KP=LDL^{\mathsf T},\] provided every prescribed pivot is nonsingular. The fixed sequence permits symbolic storage and work estimates to be reused. It does not itself guarantee bounded multipliers: if a prescribed pivot is too small, a solver must accept possible instability, perturb or regularize that pivot, or abandon the static policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static pivoting fixes ordering and pivot blocks in advance, enabling predictable sparsity but requiring acceptable or regularized pivots.
knowledge_statements.title: Static Pivoting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The description is plausible and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but static-pivoting conventions vary among sparse indefinite solvers, particularly regarding predetermined block structure and numerical perturbation. An inspectable specialized source is required.

children.title: Threshold Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Numerical pivot acceptance governed by stability thresholds.

assumptions_latex: Candidate pivots are restricted to nonsingular \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) blocks
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only pivots satisfying the threshold test are eliminated, limiting multipliers according to the chosen test.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: threshold pivoting accepts pivots by comparison with competing active entries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic threshold test for symmetric-indefinite LDL pivot selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each elimination step, let \(S\) be the active symmetric Schur complement and let \(\tau\in(0,1]\). For a candidate principal pivot block \(B=S_{I,I}\), where \(|I|\in\{1,2\}\), form \(C=S_{J,I}\) with \(J\) the remaining indices. Accept the pivot only if \(B\) is nonsingular and \[\lVert CB^{-1}\rVert_{\max}\le \tau^{-1}.\] If accepted, append \(B\) to \(D\), append \(CB^{-1}\) to \(L\), and update \(S_{J,J}\leftarrow S_{J,J}-CB^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}\). Otherwise test another candidate or delay the indices in \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Threshold pivoting accepts a candidate block only when its induced multipliers satisfy a prescribed bound; otherwise it searches or delays.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Pivoting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed multiplier-bound test defines a coherent threshold-pivoting variant and the update is dimensionally consistent. Because this is a particular norm-based acceptance rule rather than a source-neutral definition of all threshold pivoting, it requires a citation supporting that exact variant.

children.title: Delayed Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Deferral of unsuitable pivots to later frontal or elimination stages.

assumptions_latex: A specified pivot-acceptance test is used
At least one acceptable pivot block is eventually available or singularity is reported
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rejected indices remain active and are reconsidered in a later elimination front.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: delayed pivoting postpones numerically unacceptable candidates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Postponement of unstable pivots in sparse frontal LDL factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When a candidate principal block \(S_{I,I}\) fails the prescribed nonsingularity or stability test, do not eliminate its indices. Move those indices and their assembled rows and columns to the contribution passed to a later elimination front. Continue eliminating acceptable pivots from the current front, then reassemble every delayed index with additional matrix contributions and test it again. The process terminates when all indices have been pivoted or structural or numerical singularity is declared. Delaying preserves the acceptance criterion but can enlarge later fronts, increase fill and work, and make the final numerical pivot order differ from the symbolic order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed pivoting postpones unstable indices for reconsideration in a later, larger front, trading numerical stability for less predictable fill and work.
knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Pivoting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record accurately describes the intended multifrontal delayed-pivot workflow and its fill/work tradeoff, but it has no inspectable source for the specialized claims about passing delayed rows and columns to later fronts.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{n}\) has a symmetric-pivoted factorization \[P^{\mathsf T}KP=LDL^{\mathsf T},\] with nonsingular \(L\) and symmetric block-diagonal \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_s)\), where each \(D_j\) is \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\). Then congruence invariance and block additivity give \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\operatorname{inertia}(D_j).\] Thus a scalar block contributes according to its sign, while a \(2\times2\) block contributes the signs of its two eigenvalues; zero eigenvalues identify singularity in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inertia of a symmetrically pivoted matrix equals the sum of the inertias of the small diagonal blocks in its LDL factorization.

children.title: Sparse KKT Ordering Strategies
children.top_down_role: Variable and constraint permutations used before sparse KKT factorization.

assumptions_latex: A symmetric permutation is chosen before factorization
The ordering algorithm uses the undirected sparsity graph of \(K\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordering changes fill and factorization work but not the inertia or solution of the permuted KKT system.

notation.meaning: Undirected structural graph of the KKT matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: symmetric graph orderings control elimination fill
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based symmetric orderings for sparse KKT factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate a vertex with each row and column of sparse \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{n}\), and join vertices whose off-diagonal entry is structurally nonzero. A sparse KKT ordering selects a permutation \(P\) using this graph, for example by approximate minimum degree, nested dissection, or a constraint-aware block rule, before factoring \(P^{\mathsf T}KP\). The permutation should reduce predicted fill, frontal sizes, or elimination-tree work while respecting any pivoting constraints. Because \(P\) is orthogonal, symmetric reordering preserves eigenvalues, inertia, and the linear-system solution after inverse permutation; only the factor sparsity, data movement, and numerical pivot opportunities change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph-based symmetric orderings seek less fill and work in sparse KKT factors while preserving the underlying system and inertia.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse KKT Ordering Strategies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordering principle fits the terminal container and correctly distinguishes invariants of symmetric permutation from changes in fill, work, and pivot opportunities. No inspectable sparse-factorization or sparse-KKT source is supplied.

children.title: Symbolic Fill Structure
children.top_down_role: Predicted nonzero growth and elimination structure arising from a chosen ordering.

assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{n}\) has a fixed structural sparsity pattern
A symmetric elimination ordering \(\pi\) is fixed
No numerical cancellation is used in the symbolic model
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symbolic factor pattern is the filled elimination graph generated by eliminating vertices in order \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: Undirected structural graph of the matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elimination graphs characterize symbolic Cholesky and LDL fill
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cancellation-free graph model of fill under a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(K)\) be the undirected graph of the structural off-diagonal nonzeros of \(K\), and fix an ordering \(\pi\). Symbolically eliminate vertices in that order. Immediately before removing a vertex, connect every pair of its remaining neighbors. The original edges together with all edges added by this rule form the filled graph \(G_{\pi}^{+}\). Under the cancellation-free symbolic model, an entry below the diagonal is allocated in the triangular factor exactly when its corresponding ordered vertex pair is an edge of \(G_{\pi}^{+}\). Hence symbolic fill, column counts, and the elimination tree depend only on the structural pattern and \(\pi\), not on numerical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symbolic elimination connects each eliminated vertex's remaining neighbors; the resulting filled graph determines the allocated sparse factor pattern.
knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Fill Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The filled-graph characterization is standard for cancellation-free symbolic elimination under a fixed scalar ordering, but no source is cited. In this symmetric-indefinite KKT context, a source must also clarify whether the claimed factor pattern assumes scalar pivots or how fixed two-by-two pivot blocks are represented.

A symmetric permutation \(P\) is fixed before numerical factorization.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible symmetric permutation \(P\), let \(PKP^{\top}=LDL^{\top}\) be its sparse factorization. An ordering \(P_1\) is unambiguously preferable to \(P_2\) only if it dominates the relevant costs, for example \(\operatorname{fill}(P_1)\leq\operatorname{fill}(P_2)\), \(\operatorname{flop}(P_1)\leq\operatorname{flop}(P_2)\), and \(t_{\mathrm{ord}}(P_1)\leq t_{\mathrm{ord}}(P_2)\), with at least one strict inequality. Otherwise selection is a tradeoff: minimizing symbolic fill alone need not minimize total solve time or memory traffic.

children.title: Frontal KKT Solves
children.top_down_role: Sparse KKT factorization organized around individual evolving frontal matrices.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is sparse, symmetric, and permuted according to an elimination ordering.
Numerical pivots chosen inside each front are nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assembled frontal eliminations produce a direct factorization and solve for \(Kx=b\).

notation.meaning: active frontal matrix at elimination step j
Schur-complement contribution passed from front j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical frontal factorization of an ordered symmetric-indefinite KKT system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Kx=b\), process the ordered rows and columns sequentially. At step \(j\), assemble into \(F_j\) all original entries whose indices have become active together with the preceding contribution \(U_{j-1}\). Factor every fully summed pivot block of \(F_j\), form its Schur complement \(U_j\) on the remaining active variables, and discard eliminated data. After all fronts are processed, solve by forward substitution through the stored elimination factors and backward substitution through their transposes; output the resulting \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frontal solver assembles one evolving dense front, eliminates fully assembled variables, passes a Schur contribution forward, and then applies the stored factors.
